slides.title: Separate infection, active disease, infectiousness, and resistance
slides.section: Separate infection, active disease, infectiousness, and resistance
paragraphs: Resident core · 30–45 minutes with discussion

By the end, decide when to isolate, choose the first diagnostic specimens, recognize the standard treatment pathways, and explain why a positive immune test does not establish active TB. Work through three cases before using the advanced drug, special-population, and trial sections.
Keep four questions separate: has the patient been infected, is there active disease, could they transmit it now, and which drugs are likely to work? One test rarely answers all four.

slides.title: Protect others while obtaining specimens that can establish the diagnosis
slides.section: Protect others while obtaining specimens that can establish the diagnosis
paragraphs: With suspected infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB, initiate airborne precautions and involve infection prevention and the TB program. Use the institutional pathway for de-isolation; neither a negative IGRA nor one negative respiratory test is a universal clearance rule.

Obtain chest imaging and respiratory specimens for AFB smear and mycobacterial culture, with a TB NAAT on an initial specimen. The usual U.S. collection approach uses three specimens separated by 8–24 hours, including an early-morning specimen. Induced sputum or bronchoscopy may be needed when the patient cannot provide an adequate sample.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Protect others while obtaining specimens that can establish the diagnosis With suspected infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB, initiate airborne precautions and involve infection prevention and the TB program. Use the institutional pathway for de-isolation; neither a negative IGRA nor one negative respiratory test is a universal clearance rule. Obtain chest imaging and respiratory specimens for AFB smear and mycobacterial culture, with a TB NAAT on an initial specimen. The usual U.S. collection approach uses three specimens separated by 8–24 hours, including an early-morning specimen. Induced sputum or bronchoscopy may be needed when the patient cannot provide an adequate sample. AFB smear can support infectiousness assessment but does not identify M. tuberculosis by itself. NAAT can rapidly support TB and, on some platforms, identify resistance markers. A negative NAAT does not exclude all paucibacillary disease. Culture and susceptibility testing remain necessary. For extrapulmonary disease, sample the involved site and tell the laboratory what is suspected. Plan tissue handling before the biopsy so that the entire specimen is not placed in formalin. In severe illness, do not let a prolonged diagnostic process delay appropriate multidrug treatment. Sources: diagnosis , dx-guideline , ip .

slides.title: Interpret immune tests and mimics in their clinical context
slides.section: Interpret immune tests and mimics in their clinical context
rows: Positive IGRA or tuberculin skin test
Supports TB infection; does not distinguish latent infection from active disease.
Assess symptoms and imaging, and obtain microbiology when disease is possible before preventive treatment.
Does not exclude active TB, particularly with immunosuppression or recent exposure.
Continue the active-disease evaluation when suspicion remains high.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Interpret immune tests and mimics in their clinical context What the result can establish Finding Interpretation Next decision Positive IGRA or tuberculin skin test Supports TB infection; does not distinguish latent infection from active disease. Assess symptoms and imaging, and obtain microbiology when disease is possible before preventive treatment. Negative immune test Does not exclude active TB, particularly with immunosuppression or recent exposure. Continue the active-disease evaluation when suspicion remains high. AFB smear positive, TB NAAT negative Could represent NTM, a testing limitation, or another discordant result. Review specimen quality and repeat/confirm testing with the laboratory; do not equate every AFB isolate with TB. Cavity or granulomatous pathology Neither finding is specific for TB. Consider endemic fungi, NTM, malignancy, bacterial abscess, and inflammatory disease using exposure and host clues. In Missouri, histoplasmosis is an important alternative diagnosis. Avoid a “TB versus nothing” differential. A positive NTM culture also needs clinical, radiographic, and microbiologic interpretation before committing to prolonged NTM therapy. Sources: igra , tst , ntm , histo .

slides.title: Monitor response, toxicity, interactions, and the ability to complete treatment
slides.section: Monitor response, toxicity, interactions, and the ability to complete treatment
rows: Review baseline risk and liver tests when indicated. New anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, or jaundice needs prompt assessment; do not simply reassure the patient to finish the drugs.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Monitor response, toxicity, interactions, and the ability to complete treatment Safety checks during treatment Issue Practical action Hepatic injury Review baseline risk and liver tests when indicated. New anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, or jaundice needs prompt assessment; do not simply reassure the patient to finish the drugs. Ethambutol toxicity Assess baseline visual acuity and color discrimination and ask about vision changes during treatment. Renal impairment changes exposure. Isoniazid neuropathy Provide pyridoxine for patients at risk, including pregnancy, HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, and renal failure. Rifamycin interactions Review ART, anticoagulants, anticonvulsants, transplant drugs, and hormonal contraception. A rifamycin substitution still needs an interaction check. Microbiologic response Track sputum culture conversion and clinical response. Persistently positive cultures require adherence, absorption, resistance, and source reassessment. Completion Coordinate public-health reporting, adherence support, medication access, and observed therapy as appropriate. Completion is based on the prescribed doses and permitted time window, not the calendar alone. Do not withhold ART until all TB treatment is complete. ART timing depends on CD4 count, the TB site, and interactions; TB meningitis is a separate timing decision. Detailed recommendations are in the advanced section. Sources: ds , nih-tb .

slides.title: Exclude active disease before choosing preventive treatment
slides.section: Exclude active disease before choosing preventive treatment
paragraphs: A patient with latent TB infection has evidence of infection without active disease. Choose a preventive regimen only after the active-disease assessment is adequate. CDC preferentially recommends short rifamycin-based options when suitable, such as three months of weekly isoniazid-rifapentine, four months of daily rifampin, or three months of daily isoniazid-rifampin.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Exclude active disease before choosing preventive treatment A patient with latent TB infection has evidence of infection without active disease. Choose a preventive regimen only after the active-disease assessment is adequate. CDC preferentially recommends short rifamycin-based options when suitable, such as three months of weekly isoniazid-rifapentine, four months of daily rifampin, or three months of daily isoniazid-rifampin. Check pregnancy, age, HIV treatment, drug interactions, and the presumed source isolate. Isoniazid-only courses remain alternatives when a short regimen cannot be used. A drug-resistant contact needs specialist selection based on the source isolate, not automatic routine latent-TB treatment. Reassess symptoms, adherence, and adverse effects during preventive treatment. Patients should know which symptoms require stopping medication and calling the treating team. slides.title: Exclude active disease before choosing preventive treatment
slides.section: Exclude active disease before choosing preventive treatment
paragraphs: Check pregnancy, age, HIV treatment, drug interactions, and the presumed source isolate. Isoniazid-only courses remain alternatives when a short regimen cannot be used. A drug-resistant contact needs specialist selection based on the source isolate, not automatic routine latent-TB treatment.
Reassess symptoms, adherence, and adverse effects during preventive treatment. Patients should know which symptoms require stopping medication and calling the treating team.
Sources: ltbi , ltbi-guideline .
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Exclude active disease before choosing preventive treatment A patient with latent TB infection has evidence of infection without active disease. Choose a preventive regimen only after the active-disease assessment is adequate. CDC preferentially recommends short rifamycin-based options when suitable, such as three months of weekly isoniazid-rifapentine, four months of daily rifampin, or three months of daily isoniazid-rifampin. Check pregnancy, age, HIV treatment, drug interactions, and the presumed source isolate. Isoniazid-only courses remain alternatives when a short regimen cannot be used. A drug-resistant contact needs specialist selection based on the source isolate, not automatic routine latent-TB treatment. Reassess symptoms, adherence, and adverse effects during preventive treatment. Patients should know which symptoms require stopping medication and calling the treating team. Sources: ltbi , ltbi-guideline .

slides.title: Case 1 · The immune test is not the disease diagnosis
slides.section: Use three cases to connect the test result to the next step
paragraphs: An asymptomatic patient has a positive IGRA before starting a TNF inhibitor.
Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use three cases to connect the test result to the next step Case 1 · The immune test is not the disease diagnosis An asymptomatic patient has a positive IGRA before starting a TNF inhibitor. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Assess symptoms and chest imaging and investigate any concern for active disease before selecting preventive treatment. Do not label this active TB from the IGRA alone, and do not begin a preventive regimen while an unexplained pulmonary syndrome is still being evaluated. Case 2 · A negative result does not close the case A patient with weight loss, cough, an upper-lobe cavity, and immunosuppression has a negative IGRA. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Continue airborne precautions and the respiratory microbiologic evaluation. The negative immune test does not rule out active disease. Simultaneously investigate credible mimics and obtain specimens that can distinguish them. Case 3 · Resistance requires a regimen decision A respiratory NAAT detects M. tuberculosis and a rifampin-resistance marker. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Treat the result as urgent. Contact the TB program and an experienced clinician, obtain expanded susceptibility testing, and select a complete active regimen. Do not continue the standard plan unchanged or append a single new drug.

slides.title: Discussion
slides.section: Use three cases to connect the test result to the next step
paragraphs: Treat the result as urgent. Contact the TB program and an experienced clinician, obtain expanded susceptibility testing, and select a complete active regimen. Do not continue the standard plan unchanged or append a single new drug.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Use three cases to connect the test result to the next step Case 1 · The immune test is not the disease diagnosis An asymptomatic patient has a positive IGRA before starting a TNF inhibitor. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Assess symptoms and chest imaging and investigate any concern for active disease before selecting preventive treatment. Do not label this active TB from the IGRA alone, and do not begin a preventive regimen while an unexplained pulmonary syndrome is still being evaluated. Case 2 · A negative result does not close the case A patient with weight loss, cough, an upper-lobe cavity, and immunosuppression has a negative IGRA. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Continue airborne precautions and the respiratory microbiologic evaluation. The negative immune test does not rule out active disease. Simultaneously investigate credible mimics and obtain specimens that can distinguish them. Case 3 · Resistance requires a regimen decision A respiratory NAAT detects M. tuberculosis and a rifampin-resistance marker. Discuss the next action and the finding that would change it. Discussion Treat the result as urgent. Contact the TB program and an experienced clinician, obtain expanded susceptibility testing, and select a complete active regimen. Do not continue the standard plan unchanged or append a single new drug.

slides.title: Choose the regimen for the patient, organism, and disease site
slides.section: Choose the regimen for the patient, organism, and disease site
paragraphs: TB treatment is more than a prescription for four drugs. The first decisions are whether disease is active, whether the patient may transmit it, what resistance is present, and whether the evidence for a particular regimen applies to this patient.

This module is intended for internal medicine residents, ID fellows and attending physicians. The resident core is designed for 30–45 minutes; evidence details are optional. Cases are fictional teaching examples.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Choose the regimen for the patient, organism, and disease site TB treatment is more than a prescription for four drugs. The first decisions are whether disease is active, whether the patient may transmit it, what resistance is present, and whether the evidence for a particular regimen applies to this patient. This module is intended for internal medicine residents, ID fellows and attending physicians. The resident core is designed for 30–45 minutes; evidence details are optional. Cases are fictional teaching examples. Separate TB infection from disease and common mimics; select diagnostic tests and infection-prevention actions. Select a standard or shortened regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB and identify reasons to use a different course. Distinguish BPaLM, BPaL and newer WHO regimens for resistant TB. Select preventive treatment for latent TB and build a toxicity, interaction, microbiology and follow-up plan. Critique newer treatment studies using population, comparator, endpoint, effect size and limitations. Resident pathway Read the initial approach, diagnostics, mimics, prevention, drug-susceptible and resistant-TB sections, drug monitoring, cases and rounds summary. Be able to explain the regimen and what would change it. Fellow pathway Add the evidence review and special-population discussion. Pay particular attention to trial eligibility, the distinction between regimen and strategy trials, resistance mechanisms, and how drug toxicity can weaken a regimen. Attending review pathway Start with diagnostic discordance and mimics, then review shortened-regimen eligibility, resistant-TB options, preventive care and the trial tables. Use the cases to ask which finding would change the plan. Allow 30–40 minutes for a focused update or 80–105 minutes for the full primer. Version 1.1, September 15, 2026. Sources checked September 15, 2026. Educational synthesis prepared with AI assistance. Specialty review is pending. This module is educational and does not establish treatment or isolation policy.

slides.title: The clinical spectrum
slides.section: Protect others and establish the diagnosis while planning treatment
paragraphs: Inhaled M. tuberculosis can cause infection without symptoms or evidence of disease. Latent TB infection is not contagious. Progression to disease may follow recent acquisition or occur years later, particularly with impaired immunity. Pulmonary and laryngeal disease drive most transmission; extrapulmonary disease can coexist with an infectious pulmonary focus. Treat infection to prevent progression, and treat disease with an adequate combination to cure it and prevent resistance. [5]
Recognize Symptoms, exposures, immune status and imaging.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Protect others and establish the diagnosis while planning treatment The clinical spectrum Inhaled M. tuberculosis can cause infection without symptoms or evidence of disease. Latent TB infection is not contagious. Progression to disease may follow recent acquisition or occur years later, particularly with impaired immunity. Pulmonary and laryngeal disease drive most transmission; extrapulmonary disease can coexist with an infectious pulmonary focus. Treat infection to prevent progression, and treat disease with an adequate combination to cure it and prevent resistance. [5] Recognize Symptoms, exposures, immune status and imaging. Isolate Airborne precautions when pulmonary or laryngeal TB is suspected. Sample AFB smear, culture, NAAT and resistance testing. Treat Active multidrug therapy when indicated. Coordinate ID, infection prevention and public health. Cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis or compatible imaging should prompt consideration of TB. Advanced immunosuppression can produce atypical pulmonary findings or disseminated disease. An IGRA or TST measures immune sensitization. It does not distinguish latent infection from disease, establish infectiousness, or exclude active TB when negative. [5] [22] Obtain three sputum specimens for AFB smear and mycobacterial culture, generally 8-24 hours apart with at least one early-morning specimen. Send a respiratory NAAT on at least one specimen and request rapid molecular resistance testing as appropriate. Induced sputum or bronchoscopy may be needed if adequate sputum cannot be obtained. AFB smear positivity is not specific for M. tuberculosis ; culture and organism identification still matter. [5] A positive NAAT can accelerate treatment and public-health action. A negative result does not independently exclude smear-negative TB. Obtain cultures for susceptibility testing and treatment monitoring even when NAAT is positive. If the patient is seriously ill or suspicion is high, obtain specimens promptly and start an appropriate multidrug regimen without waiting weeks for culture. [5] [2] Airborne precautions are a separate decision Use an airborne infection isolation room and appropriate respiratory protection. Mask the patient for necessary transport. The traditional CDC hospital pathway includes three negative AFB smears, but its application differs between a patient being evaluated for TB and one with confirmed infectious TB. Confirmed disease also requires assessment of effective treatment and clinical improvement. Persistent suspicion, resistance, or inadequate treatment changes the decision. Follow the current institutional NAAT-based or smear-based pathway with infection prevention; neither one negative test nor a fixed number of treatment days guarantees clearance. [6] Notify the local/state TB program promptly for suspected or confirmed disease. Coordinate contact evaluation, reporting and discharge planning. Do not leave the first public-health call until discharge. [7] [6]

Complete source section:
Use each diagnostic test to answer the right question Infection, disease and infectiousness are different questions Question Useful evidence Common mistake Has infection occurred? Exposure history plus IGRA or TST in someone for whom testing is indicated. Calling a positive immune test active TB, or using a negative result to exclude disease. Is there TB disease now? Symptoms, examination, imaging and microbiology from the involved site. Treating an abnormal CT or granulomas as organism identification. Which drugs will work? Rapid molecular resistance testing followed by culture-based DST as needed. Assuming rifampin susceptibility proves susceptibility to every regimen component. Can this patient transmit TB? Disease site, respiratory burden, cough, treatment effectiveness and the institutional isolation pathway. Equating an IGRA result or a single negative sputum test with clearance. A chest radiograph is a starting point; CT can clarify cavities, nodules, adenopathy or a sampling target. Upper-lobe cavitation is suggestive but neither required nor specific. Advanced HIV may produce little cavitation, lower-zone disease or even a deceptively unrevealing radiograph. Imaging cannot reliably distinguish active from healed infection by itself. [5] [22] Respiratory smear and NAAT: interpret the combination Smear / NAAT Interpretation Next action Positive / positive Strong presumptive evidence of pulmonary TB. Treat and coordinate public health; retain culture and DST. Positive / negative NTM becomes more likely; consider assay inhibition or specimen issues. Discuss with the laboratory, obtain additional specimens and identify the organism. Reassess precautions with IP in clinical context. Negative / positive Can support presumptive TB when suspicion is meaningful. Do not dismiss the NAAT because the smear is negative; obtain cultures and resistance information. Negative / negative Does not exclude paucibacillary or smear-negative disease. Reassess pretest probability, specimen quality and alternative diagnoses; repeat or sample another site when warranted. Prefer induced sputum before bronchoscopy when a patient cannot expectorate or initial expectorated testing is unrevealing. If bronchoscopy is needed, send appropriate BAL specimens and collect post-bronchoscopy sputum. Plan specimen handling with the laboratory before an invasive procedure. [29] Extrapulmonary disease: sample the involved compartment Choosing specimens beyond sputum Presentation Specimens and complementary tests Pitfall Lymphadenopathy or focal tissue lesion Aspirate or biopsy for mycobacterial culture, NAAT where validated, and histopathology. Send a fresh sterile portion for microbiology; a specimen entirely in formalin cannot be cultured. Pleural disease Pleural fluid cells/chemistry, culture and appropriate molecular testing; consider pleural biopsy if fluid testing is nondiagnostic. ADA may support the diagnosis in context but is not organism-specific; negative fluid tests do not reliably exclude TB. Meningitis CSF opening pressure, cells, glucose/protein, mycobacterial culture and molecular testing; evaluate for other infections. Low organism burden limits sensitivity. A negative CSF result must not delay treatment when the clinical suspicion is high. Disseminated, bone/joint or genitourinary disease Target accessible tissue, aspirate, urine or other involved sites; obtain respiratory specimens if pulmonary involvement is possible. One negative compartment does not exclude disease elsewhere; alert the laboratory to the suspected diagnosis. Interpret pathology alongside microbiology: necrotizing granulomas raise suspicion but can occur with fungi and NTM; nonnecrotizing granulomas do not rule out TB. Negative extrapulmonary smear, culture or NAAT results are often insufficient to exclude disease. [29] [34] IGRA and TST: useful for infection, weak shortcuts for disease IGRA avoids BCG-related false positivity and is generally preferred for BCG-vaccinated people aged at least 5 years. An indeterminate, borderline or invalid result is not a negative test; repeat testing or TST may help after reviewing immune status and collection issues. Recent infection may not yet be detectable: repeat contact testing 8–10 weeks after the last exposure when indicated. Do not order serial IGRAs to demonstrate treatment response. Use each diagnostic test to answer the right question Infection, disease and infectiousness are different questions Question Useful evidence Common mistake Has infection occurred? Exposure history plus IGRA or TST in someone for whom testing is indicated. Calling a positive immune test active TB, or using a negative result to exclude disease. Is there TB disease now? Symptoms, examination, imaging and microbiology from the involved site. Treating an abnormal CT or granulomas as organism identification. Which drugs will work? Rapid molecular resistance testing followed by culture-based DST as needed. Assuming rifampin susceptibility proves susceptibility to every regimen component. Can this patient transmit TB? Disease site, respiratory burden, cough, treatment effectiveness and the institutional isolation pathway. Equating an IGRA result or a single negative sputum test with clearance. A chest radiograph is a starting point; CT can clarify cavities, nodules, adenopathy or a sampling target. Upper-lobe cavitation is suggestive but neither required nor specific. Advanced HIV may produce little cavitation, lower-zone disease or even a deceptively unrevealing radiograph. Imaging cannot reliably distinguish active from healed infection by itself. [5] [22] Respiratory smear and NAAT: interpret the combination Smear / NAAT Interpretation Next action Positive / positive Strong presumptive evidence of pulmonary TB. Treat and coordinate public health; retain culture and DST. Positive / negative NTM becomes more likely; consider assay inhibition or specimen issues. Negative / negative Does not exclude paucibacillary or smear-negative disease. Reassess pretest probability, specimen quality and alternative diagnoses; repeat or sample another site when warranted. slides.title: Extrapulmonary disease: sample the involved compartment
slides.section: Use each diagnostic test to answer the right question
paragraphs: Interpret pathology alongside microbiology: necrotizing granulomas raise suspicion but can occur with fungi and NTM; nonnecrotizing granulomas do not rule out TB. Negative extrapulmonary smear, culture or NAAT results are often insufficient to exclude disease. [29] [34]

Complete source section:
Use each diagnostic test to answer the right question Infection, disease and infectiousness are different questions Question Useful evidence Common mistake Has infection occurred? Exposure history plus IGRA or TST in someone for whom testing is indicated. Calling a positive immune test active TB, or using a negative result to exclude disease. Is there TB disease now? Symptoms, examination, imaging and microbiology from the involved site. Treating an abnormal CT or granulomas as organism identification. Which drugs will work? Rapid molecular resistance testing followed by culture-based DST as needed. Assuming rifampin susceptibility proves susceptibility to every regimen component. Can this patient transmit TB? Disease site, respiratory burden, cough, treatment effectiveness and the institutional isolation pathway. Equating an IGRA result or a single negative sputum test with clearance. A chest radiograph is a starting point; CT can clarify cavities, nodules, adenopathy or a sampling target. Upper-lobe cavitation is suggestive but neither required nor specific. Advanced HIV may produce little cavitation, lower-zone disease or even a deceptively unrevealing radiograph. Imaging cannot reliably distinguish active from healed infection by itself. [5] [22] Respiratory smear and NAAT: interpret the combination Smear / NAAT Interpretation Next action Positive / positive Strong presumptive evidence of pulmonary TB. Treat and coordinate public health; retain culture and DST. Positive / negative NTM becomes more likely; consider assay inhibition or specimen issues. Discuss with the laboratory, obtain additional specimens and identify the organism. Reassess precautions with IP in clinical context. Negative / negative Does not exclude paucibacillary or smear-negative disease. Reassess pretest probability, specimen quality and alternative diagnoses; repeat or sample another site when warranted. Prefer induced sputum before bronchoscopy when a patient cannot expectorate or initial expectorated testing is unrevealing. If bronchoscopy is needed, send appropriate BAL specimens and collect post-bronchoscopy sputum. Plan specimen handling with the laboratory before an invasive procedure. Send a fresh sterile portion for microbiology; a specimen entirely in formalin cannot be cultured. Pleural disease Pleural fluid cells/chemistry, culture and appropriate molecular testing; consider pleural biopsy if fluid testing is nondiagnostic. ADA may support the diagnosis in context but is not organism-specific; negative fluid tests do not reliably exclude TB. A negative CSF result must not delay treatment when the clinical suspicion is high. Disseminated, bone/joint or genitourinary disease Target accessible tissue, aspirate, urine or other involved sites; obtain respiratory specimens if pulmonary involvement is possible. One negative compartment does not exclude disease elsewhere; alert the laboratory to the suspected diagnosis. slides.title: Keep a competing diagnosis until the evidence separates it from TB
slides.section: Keep a competing diagnosis until the evidence separates it from TB
paragraphs: A positive IGRA can coexist with cancer, fungal infection or bacterial pneumonia. It does not explain a cavity, lymph node or constitutional syndrome. Ask whether the proposed diagnosis accounts for the time course, immune status, exposures and microbiology.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Keep a competing diagnosis until the evidence separates it from TB A positive IGRA can coexist with cancer, fungal infection or bacterial pneumonia. It does not explain a cavity, lymph node or constitutional syndrome. Ask whether the proposed diagnosis accounts for the time course, immune status, exposures and microbiology. TB mimics and the next discriminating step Mimic Clues that shift the differential Useful next step NTM, including MAC and M. kansasii Structural lung disease, bronchiectasis/nodules or cavities; AFB-positive samples with a negative TB NAAT. Speciation and repeated cultures. Require compatible clinical/radiographic findings and microbiologic criteria, not an isolated sputum result. Histoplasmosis and other endemic fungi Geography, travel, soil/bird/bat exposure or immunosuppression; nodules, nodes, cavities or dissemination. Select fungal antigen, antibody, culture and tissue tests for the syndrome. Histoplasma antigen cross-reacts with Blastomyces; negative early testing may need repetition. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis Pre-existing cavity, chronic symptoms, pleural thickening or a fungal ball. Aspergillus serology and respiratory testing interpreted with imaging and duration. Bacterial lung abscess or septic emboli Aspiration/dental risk, acute toxicity, bacteremia, endocarditis risk or multiple peripheral cavities. Routine cultures, blood cultures when indicated and evaluation of the relevant anatomic or endovascular source. Nocardia Immunosuppression with nodules/cavities; possible CNS dissemination. Alert microbiology to suspected Nocardia and obtain organism identification; evaluate dissemination as appropriate. Malignancy Smoking history, progressive focal lesion, obstruction or persistent adenopathy. Obtain cytology/tissue when indicated; a positive TB infection test must not close the cancer workup. GPA or other inflammatory disease Pulmonary nodules/cavities with ENT, renal or systemic inflammatory findings; sarcoidosis may cause adenopathy/granulomas. Urinalysis, directed serology and tissue in context. Evaluate infection before escalating immunosuppression. [32] [33] [34] NTM pulmonary disease generally requires the same species in at least two separately collected sputum cultures, or a qualifying bronchoscopic or biopsy result, alongside compatible illness and imaging and exclusion of alternatives. Meeting diagnostic criteria does not automatically require treatment; species, progression and patient priorities matter. Do not apply an empiric TB regimen to all AFB-positive disease. [32] Attending checkpoint If the patient is not improving, reconsider the diagnosis before reflexively extending treatment. Review adherence, drug exposure, resistance, a second infection or malignancy, and paradoxical inflammation. Clinical deterioration is a reason to reassess and resample, not proof of either resistance or IRIS.

Routine cultures, blood cultures when indicated and evaluation of the relevant anatomic or endovascular source. Nocardia Immunosuppression with nodules/cavities; possible CNS dissemination. Alert microbiology to suspected Nocardia and obtain organism identification; evaluate dissemination as appropriate. Malignancy Smoking history, progressive focal lesion, obstruction or persistent adenopathy. Obtain cytology/tissue when indicated; a positive TB infection test must not close the cancer workup. GPA or other inflammatory disease Pulmonary nodules/cavities with ENT, renal or systemic inflammatory findings; sarcoidosis may cause adenopathy/granulomas. slides.title: Six-month therapy remains useful, and selected patients can receive four months
slides.section: Six-month therapy remains useful, and selected patients can receive four months
rows: H = isoniazid, R = rifampin, Z = pyrazinamide, E = ethambutol. Give HRZE for the initial 2 months, then HR for 4 months. Daily dosing is preferred.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Six-month therapy remains useful, and selected patients can receive four months Drug-susceptible treatment choices Clinical situation Regimen Practical interpretation Usual drug-susceptible pulmonary TB 2HRZE/4HR H = isoniazid, R = rifampin, Z = pyrazinamide, E = ethambutol. Give HRZE for the initial 2 months, then HR for 4 months. Daily dosing is preferred. Eligible adolescent or adult with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB 2HPZM/2HPM, a 17-week course P = rifapentine, M = moxifloxacin. Initial 8 weeks of HPZM, then 9 weeks of HPM. This changes both the rifamycin and companion drug; it is not four months of RIPE. Cavitation plus a positive culture at completion of 2 months on the standard regimen Usually 2HRZE/7HR, 9 months total Both features together support extension. Review adherence, susceptibility and response rather than extending every cavitary case automatically. Pyrazinamide omitted or ineffective Usually a 9-month rifamycin/isoniazid-based course Initial ethambutol is used while susceptibility is clarified. PZA-resistant disease, including typical M. bovis, needs a revised plan. Selected child with nonsevere drug-susceptible TB 2HRZ(E)/2HR, 4 months A separate pediatric recommendation for ages 3 months to 16 years. Nonsevere criteria and pediatric dosing must be checked; this is not the adult rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen. [3] [1] [2] Ethambutol protects the initial regimen while susceptibility is unknown. It can be stopped once isoniazid and rifampin susceptibility is established and the treatment plan remains appropriate. Count completed doses and interruptions, not simply elapsed calendar time. [2] Before choosing rifapentine-moxifloxacin Confirm pulmonary disease, age at least 12 years, weight at least 40 kg, no known or suspected resistance to a component, and acceptable interactions and QT risk. For people with HIV, CDC implementation guidance specifies CD4 counts at least 100 cells/µL and efavirenz-based ART. Do not assume that another ART regimen is compatible with daily high-dose rifapentine. The evidence does not justify routine use during pregnancy or breastfeeding, in most extrapulmonary disease, or when resistance is suspected. Prior TB therapy or recent exposure to fluoroquinolones warrants careful review. [4] The regimen is 119 daily doses with food. Isoniazid is 300 mg daily, rifapentine 1,200 mg daily and moxifloxacin 400 mg daily; pyrazinamide is weight-based during the first 8 weeks. Add pyridoxine 25-50 mg daily. Ensure the complete course, follow-up testing and observed-therapy support are available before selecting it. [4] [1] A shorter regimen is an option, not a reason to improvise If the patient cannot receive moxifloxacin, simply removing it from the four-month regimen is not supported. Similarly, stopping standard HRZE/HR at four months because sputum converted early does not reproduce Study 31. [10]

slides.section: Six-month therapy remains useful, and selected patients can receive four months

A separate pediatric recommendation for ages 3 months to 16 years. Nonsevere criteria and pediatric dosing must be checked; this is not the adult rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen.

Eligible adolescent or adult with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB 2HPZM/2HPM, a 17-week course P = rifapentine, M = moxifloxacin. Initial 8 weeks of HPZM, then 9 weeks of HPM. This changes both the rifamycin and companion drug; it is not four months of RIPE. Cavitation plus a positive culture at completion of 2 months on the standard regimen Usually 2HRZE/7HR, 9 months total Both features together support extension. slides.title: Rifampin resistance changes the entire regimen
slides.section: Rifampin resistance changes the entire regimen
paragraphs: RR-TB means rifampin-resistant TB. MDR-TB is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is a major treatment branch point. Confirm the molecular result, obtain expanded susceptibility testing, review previous TB drugs and contact a TB expert promptly. Never add one drug to a failing regimen. [7] [8]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Rifampin resistance changes the entire regimen RR-TB means rifampin-resistant TB. MDR-TB is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is a major treatment branch point. Confirm the molecular result, obtain expanded susceptibility testing, review previous TB drugs and contact a TB expert promptly. Never add one drug to a failing regimen. [7] [8] Short oral regimens for resistant TB Regimen Where it fits What needs checking BPaLM Bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid + moxifloxacin. U.S. guideline-recommended six-month option for eligible patients aged at least 14 years with rifampin-resistant, fluoroquinolone-susceptible pulmonary TB. Component activity, prior exposure, disease site, pregnancy/breastfeeding, interactions, ECG and ability to monitor linezolid toxicity. BPaL Bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid. U.S. guideline option for eligible patients aged at least 14 years with RR pulmonary TB and fluoroquinolone resistance or intolerance. Do not treat this as a universal three-drug salvage regimen. Known or suspected resistance to bedaquiline, pretomanid or linezolid can undermine it. Prior exposure of at least one month to a component requires expert review and appropriate resistance exclusion. BDLLfxC strategy Bedaquiline + delamanid + linezolid + levofloxacin + clofazimine. WHO six-month option for MDR/RR-TB, including additional fluoroquinolone resistance. Use susceptibility results to simplify to BDLLfx when FQ susceptible or BDLC when FQ resistant. WHO eligibility is broader, including children and pregnancy, but CNS, osteoarticular and disseminated multiorgan disease require other approaches. Nine-month endTB regimens WHO options include BLMZ, BCLLfxZ and BDLLfxZ for selected fluoroquinolone-susceptible MDR/RR-TB. Each is a studied combination, not a menu of interchangeable drugs. These are alternatives when six-month regimens are unsuitable; they were not compared directly with BPaLM. Individualized longer treatment For resistance, intolerance, disease sites or prior drug exposure that invalidate short-regimen eligibility. Construct a sufficiently active combination with expert input and DST. Duration depends on the actual regimen and response, not the RR label alone. [1] [8] [9] [13] Abbreviations in resistant-TB combinations: B, bedaquiline; Pa, pretomanid; L, linezolid; M, moxifloxacin; D, delamanid; Lfx, levofloxacin; C, clofazimine; Z, pyrazinamide. These letters name the full combination and do not authorize substitutions. The 2025 U.S. panel recommends 26 weeks of BPaL/BPaLM, despite the 24-week TB-PRACTECAL study regimen. The usual adult framework uses pretomanid 200 mg daily, linezolid 600 mg daily and, for BPaLM, moxifloxacin 400 mg daily. One established bedaquiline schedule is 400 mg daily for 2 weeks, then 200 mg three times weekly, separated by at least 48 hours. Use the exact selected protocol; alternative bedaquiline schedules and toxicity-driven changes should not be mixed casually. [1] Resistance is more than a rifampin result Prior bedaquiline/clofazimine or nitroimidazole exposure can matter even when the patient has never received the proposed full combination. Review molecular and phenotypic results with the reference laboratory; the availability and interpretation of newer-drug DST differ from routine antibacterial testing. Loss of linezolid to toxicity can leave too few active companion drugs. Persistent or recurrent culture positivity should prompt renewed DST and adherence/exposure review, not automatic prolongation of the same drugs. [9] [1] WHO recommendation, FDA labeling and local access are different questions. In the U.S., arrange expert consultation and access before prescribing delamanid-based or other nonstandard combinations. No local formulary availability is assumed here.

slides.title: Rifampin resistance changes the entire regimen
slides.section: Rifampin resistance changes the entire regimen
rows: WHO options include BLMZ, BCLLfxZ and BDLLfxZ for selected fluoroquinolone-susceptible MDR/RR-TB.
Each is a studied combination, not a menu of interchangeable drugs. These are alternatives when six-month regimens are unsuitable; they were not compared directly with BPaLM.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Rifampin resistance changes the entire regimen RR-TB means rifampin-resistant TB. MDR-TB is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is a major treatment branch point. Confirm the molecular result, obtain expanded susceptibility testing, review previous TB drugs and contact a TB expert promptly. Never add one drug to a failing regimen. [7] [8] Short oral regimens for resistant TB Regimen Where it fits What needs checking BPaLM Bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid + moxifloxacin. U.S. guideline-recommended six-month option for eligible patients aged at least 14 years with rifampin-resistant, fluoroquinolone-susceptible pulmonary TB. Component activity, prior exposure, disease site, pregnancy/breastfeeding, interactions, ECG and ability to monitor linezolid toxicity. BPaL Bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid. U.S. guideline option for eligible patients aged at least 14 years with RR pulmonary TB and fluoroquinolone resistance or intolerance. Do not treat this as a universal three-drug salvage regimen. Known or suspected resistance to bedaquiline, pretomanid or linezolid can undermine it. Prior exposure of at least one month to a component requires expert review and appropriate resistance exclusion. BDLLfxC strategy Bedaquiline + delamanid + linezolid + levofloxacin + clofazimine. WHO six-month option for MDR/RR-TB, including additional fluoroquinolone resistance. Use susceptibility results to simplify to BDLLfx when FQ susceptible or BDLC when FQ resistant. WHO eligibility is broader, including children and pregnancy, but CNS, osteoarticular and disseminated multiorgan disease require other approaches. Nine-month endTB regimens WHO options include BLMZ, BCLLfxZ and BDLLfxZ for selected fluoroquinolone-susceptible MDR/RR-TB. Each is a studied combination, not a menu of interchangeable drugs. These are alternatives when six-month regimens are unsuitable; they were not compared directly with BPaLM. Individualized longer treatment For resistance, intolerance, disease sites or prior drug exposure that invalidate short-regimen eligibility. Construct a sufficiently active combination with expert input and DST. Duration depends on the actual regimen and response, not the RR label alone. [1] [8] [9] [13] Abbreviations in resistant-TB combinations: B, bedaquiline; Pa, pretomanid; L, linezolid; M, moxifloxacin; D, delamanid; Lfx, levofloxacin; C, clofazimine; Z, pyrazinamide. These letters name the full combination and do not authorize substitutions. The 2025 U.S. panel recommends 26 weeks of BPaL/BPaLM, despite the 24-week TB-PRACTECAL study regimen. The usual adult framework uses pretomanid 200 mg daily, linezolid 600 mg daily and, for BPaLM, moxifloxacin 400 mg daily. One established bedaquiline schedule is 400 mg daily for 2 weeks, then 200 mg three times weekly, separated by at least 48 hours. Use the exact selected protocol; alternative bedaquiline schedules and toxicity-driven changes should not be mixed casually. [1] Resistance is more than a rifampin result Prior bedaquiline/clofazimine or nitroimidazole exposure can matter even when the patient has never received the proposed full combination. Review molecular and phenotypic results with the reference laboratory; the availability and interpretation of newer-drug DST differ from routine antibacterial testing. Loss of linezolid to toxicity can leave too few active companion drugs. Persistent or recurrent culture positivity should prompt renewed DST and adherence/exposure review, not automatic prolongation of the same drugs. [9] [1] WHO recommendation, FDA labeling and local access are different questions. In the U.S., arrange expert consultation and access before prescribing delamanid-based or other nonstandard combinations. No local formulary availability is assumed here.

slides.title: Resistance is more than a rifampin result
slides.section: Rifampin resistance changes the entire regimen
paragraphs: Prior bedaquiline/clofazimine or nitroimidazole exposure can matter even when the patient has never received the proposed full combination. Review molecular and phenotypic results with the reference laboratory; the availability and interpretation of newer-drug DST differ from routine antibacterial testing. Loss of linezolid to toxicity can leave too few active companion drugs. Persistent or recurrent culture positivity should prompt renewed DST and adherence/exposure review, not automatic prolongation of the same drugs. [9] [1]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Rifampin resistance changes the entire regimen RR-TB means rifampin-resistant TB. MDR-TB is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is a major treatment branch point. Confirm the molecular result, obtain expanded susceptibility testing, review previous TB drugs and contact a TB expert promptly. Never add one drug to a failing regimen. [7] [8] Short oral regimens for resistant TB Regimen Where it fits What needs checking BPaLM Bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid + moxifloxacin. U.S. guideline-recommended six-month option for eligible patients aged at least 14 years with rifampin-resistant, fluoroquinolone-susceptible pulmonary TB. Component activity, prior exposure, disease site, pregnancy/breastfeeding, interactions, ECG and ability to monitor linezolid toxicity. BPaL Bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid. U.S. guideline option for eligible patients aged at least 14 years with RR pulmonary TB and fluoroquinolone resistance or intolerance. Do not treat this as a universal three-drug salvage regimen. Known or suspected resistance to bedaquiline, pretomanid or linezolid can undermine it. Prior exposure of at least one month to a component requires expert review and appropriate resistance exclusion. BDLLfxC strategy Bedaquiline + delamanid + linezolid + levofloxacin + clofazimine. WHO six-month option for MDR/RR-TB, including additional fluoroquinolone resistance. Use susceptibility results to simplify to BDLLfx when FQ susceptible or BDLC when FQ resistant. WHO eligibility is broader, including children and pregnancy, but CNS, osteoarticular and disseminated multiorgan disease require other approaches. Nine-month endTB regimens WHO options include BLMZ, BCLLfxZ and BDLLfxZ for selected fluoroquinolone-susceptible MDR/RR-TB. Each is a studied combination, not a menu of interchangeable drugs. These are alternatives when six-month regimens are unsuitable; they were not compared directly with BPaLM. Individualized longer treatment For resistance, intolerance, disease sites or prior drug exposure that invalidate short-regimen eligibility. Construct a sufficiently active combination with expert input and DST. Duration depends on the actual regimen and response, not the RR label alone. [1] [8] [9] [13] Abbreviations in resistant-TB combinations: B, bedaquiline; Pa, pretomanid; L, linezolid; M, moxifloxacin; D, delamanid; Lfx, levofloxacin; C, clofazimine; Z, pyrazinamide. These letters name the full combination and do not authorize substitutions. The 2025 U.S. panel recommends 26 weeks of BPaL/BPaLM, despite the 24-week TB-PRACTECAL study regimen. The usual adult framework uses pretomanid 200 mg daily, linezolid 600 mg daily and, for BPaLM, moxifloxacin 400 mg daily. One established bedaquiline schedule is 400 mg daily for 2 weeks, then 200 mg three times weekly, separated by at least 48 hours. Use the exact selected protocol; alternative bedaquiline schedules and toxicity-driven changes should not be mixed casually. [1] Resistance is more than a rifampin result Prior bedaquiline/clofazimine or nitroimidazole exposure can matter even when the patient has never received the proposed full combination. Review molecular and phenotypic results with the reference laboratory; the availability and interpretation of newer-drug DST differ from routine antibacterial testing. Loss of linezolid to toxicity can leave too few active companion drugs. Persistent or recurrent culture positivity should prompt renewed DST and adherence/exposure review, not automatic prolongation of the same drugs. [9] [1] WHO recommendation, FDA labeling and local access are different questions. In the U.S., arrange expert consultation and access before prescribing delamanid-based or other nonstandard combinations. No local formulary availability is assumed here.

slides.title: Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen
slides.section: Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen
rows: Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. Give pyridoxine, especially with neuropathy risk; the four-month regimen uses 25-50 mg daily for all patients.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen Core adult drugs and monitoring Drug Usual adult framework Monitoring and common traps Isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily, usually 300 mg maximum Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. Give pyridoxine, especially with neuropathy risk; the four-month regimen uses 25-50 mg daily for all patients. Rifampin 10 mg/kg daily, usually 600 mg maximum Major enzyme/transporter induction. Review ART, azoles, anticoagulants, transplant drugs, methadone and hormonal contraception. Orange secretions are expected; jaundice is not. Pyrazinamide Weight-band dosing, generally about 20-25 mg/kg daily Hepatotoxicity, arthralgia and hyperuricemia. Asymptomatic hyperuricemia alone is not an indication to stop. Adjust interval in severe renal impairment. Ethambutol Weight-band dosing, generally 15-20 mg/kg daily Baseline visual acuity and color discrimination, then symptom surveillance and repeat testing according to duration/risk. Stop and evaluate new visual symptoms. Accumulates with renal impairment. Rifapentine 1,200 mg daily in the 17-week active-TB regimen Do not confuse with the weekly dose/frequency used in 3HP prevention. Review interactions; give with food. Moxifloxacin / levofloxacin Moxifloxacin 400 mg daily in HPMZ/BPaLM; levofloxacin dosing depends on weight and kidney function QT, tendinopathy, neuropathy, dysglycemia and cation binding. Correct K+ and Mg2+, assess other QT drugs. Levofloxacin needs renal adjustment. Bedaquiline Use the selected regimen’s loading and continuation schedule ECG/QTc, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, liver tests and interacting drugs. Rifamycins can markedly lower exposure. Pretomanid 200 mg daily with food within an appropriate combination Hepatic toxicity and combination-regimen adverse effects. Avoid extrapolating pulmonary-trial evidence to CNS disease or pregnancy. Linezolid Usually 600 mg daily initially in current BPaL/BPaLM CBC, peripheral neuropathy, vision and symptoms of lactic acidosis. Review serotonergic drugs. Six months is very different from a short antibacterial course. Delamanid / clofazimine Regimen-specific dosing under TB-program direction Additive QT risk. Clofazimine can cause skin discoloration and GI toxicity. Monitor the combination, not each drug in isolation. [2] [4] [1] [9] Baseline and follow-up plan Document weight, HIV status, pregnancy possibility, complete medication history, prior TB therapy and disease sites. Obtain CBC, creatinine/eGFR, AST/ALT and bilirubin, with hepatitis testing based on risk. Add baseline vision testing for ethambutol or prolonged linezolid and ECG/electrolytes for QT-active regimens. [2] [1] Review symptoms, adherence, weight and toxicity at least monthly. In pulmonary disease, obtain sputum cultures monthly until conversion is documented; the end-of-intensive-phase culture is particularly important. Continue cultures and other response assessment as required by the selected drug-resistant protocol. Smear or NAAT positivity alone is not proof of viable bacilli or failure. [2] [3] [9] For prolonged linezolid, check CBC early and frequently, commonly weekly initially, with ongoing neurologic and visual assessment. Use the published regimen-specific ECG and laboratory schedule for BPaL/BPaLM or BDLLfxC. Increase surveillance when renal dysfunction, abnormal baseline results, QT-active combinations or new symptoms raise risk. Therapeutic drug monitoring may help with toxicity, suspected malabsorption or poor response. [1] [9] New hepatitis needs a same-day plan Hold hepatotoxic TB drugs and evaluate when ALT is at least 3 times the upper limit of normal with hepatitis symptoms, or at least 5 times without symptoms. Assess bilirubin, INR and other causes. In severe disease, arrange an active nonhepatotoxic interim combination with a TB expert. Reintroduction is supervised and sequential after recovery; do not leave the patient on an accidentally ineffective partial regimen. [2] With creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min or hemodialysis, pyrazinamide and ethambutol generally require interval adjustment, often three times weekly after dialysis. Isoniazid and rifampin usually retain standard dosing. Confirm the exact weight-based dose and monitoring with pharmacy. [28] [2]

slides.title: Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen
slides.section: Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen
rows: Weight-band dosing, generally about 20-25 mg/kg daily
Hepatotoxicity, arthralgia and hyperuricemia. Asymptomatic hyperuricemia alone is not an indication to stop. Adjust interval in severe renal impairment.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen Core adult drugs and monitoring Drug Usual adult framework Monitoring and common traps Isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily, usually 300 mg maximum Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. Give pyridoxine, especially with neuropathy risk; the four-month regimen uses 25-50 mg daily for all patients. Rifampin 10 mg/kg daily, usually 600 mg maximum Major enzyme/transporter induction. Review ART, azoles, anticoagulants, transplant drugs, methadone and hormonal contraception. Orange secretions are expected; jaundice is not. Pyrazinamide Weight-band dosing, generally about 20-25 mg/kg daily Hepatotoxicity, arthralgia and hyperuricemia. Asymptomatic hyperuricemia alone is not an indication to stop. Adjust interval in severe renal impairment. Ethambutol Weight-band dosing, generally 15-20 mg/kg daily Baseline visual acuity and color discrimination, then symptom surveillance and repeat testing according to duration/risk. Stop and evaluate new visual symptoms. Accumulates with renal impairment. Rifapentine 1,200 mg daily in the 17-week active-TB regimen Do not confuse with the weekly dose/frequency used in 3HP prevention. Review interactions; give with food. Moxifloxacin / levofloxacin Moxifloxacin 400 mg daily in HPMZ/BPaLM; levofloxacin dosing depends on weight and kidney function QT, tendinopathy, neuropathy, dysglycemia and cation binding. Correct K+ and Mg2+, assess other QT drugs. Levofloxacin needs renal adjustment. Bedaquiline Use the selected regimen’s loading and continuation schedule ECG/QTc, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, liver tests and interacting drugs. Rifamycins can markedly lower exposure. Pretomanid 200 mg daily with food within an appropriate combination Hepatic toxicity and combination-regimen adverse effects. Avoid extrapolating pulmonary-trial evidence to CNS disease or pregnancy. Linezolid Usually 600 mg daily initially in current BPaL/BPaLM CBC, peripheral neuropathy, vision and symptoms of lactic acidosis. Review serotonergic drugs. Six months is very different from a short antibacterial course. Delamanid / clofazimine Regimen-specific dosing under TB-program direction Additive QT risk. Clofazimine can cause skin discoloration and GI toxicity. Monitor the combination, not each drug in isolation. [2] [4] [1] [9] Baseline and follow-up plan Document weight, HIV status, pregnancy possibility, complete medication history, prior TB therapy and disease sites. Obtain CBC, creatinine/eGFR, AST/ALT and bilirubin, with hepatitis testing based on risk. Add baseline vision testing for ethambutol or prolonged linezolid and ECG/electrolytes for QT-active regimens. [2] [1] Review symptoms, adherence, weight and toxicity at least monthly. In pulmonary disease, obtain sputum cultures monthly until conversion is documented; the end-of-intensive-phase culture is particularly important. Continue cultures and other response assessment as required by the selected drug-resistant protocol. Smear or NAAT positivity alone is not proof of viable bacilli or failure. [2] [3] [9] For prolonged linezolid, check CBC early and frequently, commonly weekly initially, with ongoing neurologic and visual assessment. Use the published regimen-specific ECG and laboratory schedule for BPaL/BPaLM or BDLLfxC. Increase surveillance when renal dysfunction, abnormal baseline results, QT-active combinations or new symptoms raise risk. Therapeutic drug monitoring may help with toxicity, suspected malabsorption or poor response. [1] [9] New hepatitis needs a same-day plan Hold hepatotoxic TB drugs and evaluate when ALT is at least 3 times the upper limit of normal with hepatitis symptoms, or at least 5 times without symptoms. Assess bilirubin, INR and other causes. In severe disease, arrange an active nonhepatotoxic interim combination with a TB expert. Reintroduction is supervised and sequential after recovery; do not leave the patient on an accidentally ineffective partial regimen. [2] With creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min or hemodialysis, pyrazinamide and ethambutol generally require interval adjustment, often three times weekly after dialysis. Isoniazid and rifampin usually retain standard dosing. Confirm the exact weight-based dose and monitoring with pharmacy. [28] [2]

slides.title: Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen
slides.section: Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen
rows: Use the selected regimen’s loading and continuation schedule
ECG/QTc, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, liver tests and interacting drugs. Rifamycins can markedly lower exposure.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen Core adult drugs and monitoring Drug Usual adult framework Monitoring and common traps Isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily, usually 300 mg maximum Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. Give pyridoxine, especially with neuropathy risk; the four-month regimen uses 25-50 mg daily for all patients. Rifampin 10 mg/kg daily, usually 600 mg maximum Major enzyme/transporter induction. Review ART, azoles, anticoagulants, transplant drugs, methadone and hormonal contraception. Orange secretions are expected; jaundice is not. Pyrazinamide Weight-band dosing, generally about 20-25 mg/kg daily Hepatotoxicity, arthralgia and hyperuricemia. Asymptomatic hyperuricemia alone is not an indication to stop. Adjust interval in severe renal impairment. Ethambutol Weight-band dosing, generally 15-20 mg/kg daily Baseline visual acuity and color discrimination, then symptom surveillance and repeat testing according to duration/risk. Stop and evaluate new visual symptoms. Accumulates with renal impairment. Rifapentine 1,200 mg daily in the 17-week active-TB regimen Do not confuse with the weekly dose/frequency used in 3HP prevention. Review interactions; give with food. Moxifloxacin / levofloxacin Moxifloxacin 400 mg daily in HPMZ/BPaLM; levofloxacin dosing depends on weight and kidney function QT, tendinopathy, neuropathy, dysglycemia and cation binding. Correct K+ and Mg2+, assess other QT drugs. Levofloxacin needs renal adjustment. Bedaquiline Use the selected regimen’s loading and continuation schedule ECG/QTc, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, liver tests and interacting drugs. Rifamycins can markedly lower exposure. Pretomanid 200 mg daily with food within an appropriate combination Hepatic toxicity and combination-regimen adverse effects. Avoid extrapolating pulmonary-trial evidence to CNS disease or pregnancy. Linezolid Usually 600 mg daily initially in current BPaL/BPaLM CBC, peripheral neuropathy, vision and symptoms of lactic acidosis. Review serotonergic drugs. Six months is very different from a short antibacterial course. Delamanid / clofazimine Regimen-specific dosing under TB-program direction Additive QT risk. Clofazimine can cause skin discoloration and GI toxicity. Monitor the combination, not each drug in isolation. [2] [4] [1] [9] Baseline and follow-up plan Document weight, HIV status, pregnancy possibility, complete medication history, prior TB therapy and disease sites. Obtain CBC, creatinine/eGFR, AST/ALT and bilirubin, with hepatitis testing based on risk. Add baseline vision testing for ethambutol or prolonged linezolid and ECG/electrolytes for QT-active regimens. [2] [1] Review symptoms, adherence, weight and toxicity at least monthly. In pulmonary disease, obtain sputum cultures monthly until conversion is documented; the end-of-intensive-phase culture is particularly important. Continue cultures and other response assessment as required by the selected drug-resistant protocol. Smear or NAAT positivity alone is not proof of viable bacilli or failure. [2] [3] [9] For prolonged linezolid, check CBC early and frequently, commonly weekly initially, with ongoing neurologic and visual assessment. Use the published regimen-specific ECG and laboratory schedule for BPaL/BPaLM or BDLLfxC. Increase surveillance when renal dysfunction, abnormal baseline results, QT-active combinations or new symptoms raise risk. Therapeutic drug monitoring may help with toxicity, suspected malabsorption or poor response. [1] [9] New hepatitis needs a same-day plan Hold hepatotoxic TB drugs and evaluate when ALT is at least 3 times the upper limit of normal with hepatitis symptoms, or at least 5 times without symptoms. Assess bilirubin, INR and other causes. In severe disease, arrange an active nonhepatotoxic interim combination with a TB expert. Reintroduction is supervised and sequential after recovery; do not leave the patient on an accidentally ineffective partial regimen. [2] With creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min or hemodialysis, pyrazinamide and ethambutol generally require interval adjustment, often three times weekly after dialysis. Isoniazid and rifampin usually retain standard dosing. Confirm the exact weight-based dose and monitoring with pharmacy. [28] [2]

Ethambutol Weight-band dosing, generally 15-20 mg/kg daily Baseline visual acuity and color discrimination, then symptom surveillance and repeat testing according to duration/risk. slides.title: New hepatitis needs a same-day plan
slides.section: Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen
paragraphs: Hold hepatotoxic TB drugs and evaluate when ALT is at least 3 times the upper limit of normal with hepatitis symptoms, or at least 5 times without symptoms. Assess bilirubin, INR and other causes. In severe disease, arrange an active nonhepatotoxic interim combination with a TB expert. Reintroduction is supervised and sequential after recovery; do not leave the patient on an accidentally ineffective partial regimen.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Monitoring should follow the toxicities of the actual regimen Core adult drugs and monitoring Drug Usual adult framework Monitoring and common traps Isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily, usually 300 mg maximum Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. Give pyridoxine, especially with neuropathy risk; the four-month regimen uses 25-50 mg daily for all patients. Rifampin 10 mg/kg daily, usually 600 mg maximum Major enzyme/transporter induction. Review ART, azoles, anticoagulants, transplant drugs, methadone and hormonal contraception. Orange secretions are expected; jaundice is not. Pyrazinamide Weight-band dosing, generally about 20-25 mg/kg daily Hepatotoxicity, arthralgia and hyperuricemia. Asymptomatic hyperuricemia alone is not an indication to stop. Adjust interval in severe renal impairment. Ethambutol Weight-band dosing, generally 15-20 mg/kg daily Baseline visual acuity and color discrimination, then symptom surveillance and repeat testing according to duration/risk. Stop and evaluate new visual symptoms. Accumulates with renal impairment. Rifapentine 1,200 mg daily in the 17-week active-TB regimen Do not confuse with the weekly dose/frequency used in 3HP prevention. Review interactions; give with food. Moxifloxacin / levofloxacin Moxifloxacin 400 mg daily in HPMZ/BPaLM; levofloxacin dosing depends on weight and kidney function QT, tendinopathy, neuropathy, dysglycemia and cation binding. Correct K+ and Mg2+, assess other QT drugs. Levofloxacin needs renal adjustment. Bedaquiline Use the selected regimen’s loading and continuation schedule ECG/QTc, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, liver tests and interacting drugs. Rifamycins can markedly lower exposure. Pretomanid 200 mg daily with food within an appropriate combination Hepatic toxicity and combination-regimen adverse effects. Avoid extrapolating pulmonary-trial evidence to CNS disease or pregnancy. Linezolid Usually 600 mg daily initially in current BPaL/BPaLM CBC, peripheral neuropathy, vision and symptoms of lactic acidosis. Review serotonergic drugs. Six months is very different from a short antibacterial course. Delamanid / clofazimine Regimen-specific dosing under TB-program direction Additive QT risk. Clofazimine can cause skin discoloration and GI toxicity. Monitor the combination, not each drug in isolation. [2] [4] [1] [9] Baseline and follow-up plan Document weight, HIV status, pregnancy possibility, complete medication history, prior TB therapy and disease sites. Obtain CBC, creatinine/eGFR, AST/ALT and bilirubin, with hepatitis testing based on risk. Add baseline vision testing for ethambutol or prolonged linezolid and ECG/electrolytes for QT-active regimens. [2] [1] Review symptoms, adherence, weight and toxicity at least monthly. In pulmonary disease, obtain sputum cultures monthly until conversion is documented; the end-of-intensive-phase culture is particularly important. Continue cultures and other response assessment as required by the selected drug-resistant protocol. Smear or NAAT positivity alone is not proof of viable bacilli or failure. [2] [3] [9] For prolonged linezolid, check CBC early and frequently, commonly weekly initially, with ongoing neurologic and visual assessment. Use the published regimen-specific ECG and laboratory schedule for BPaL/BPaLM or BDLLfxC. Increase surveillance when renal dysfunction, abnormal baseline results, QT-active combinations or new symptoms raise risk. Therapeutic drug monitoring may help with toxicity, suspected malabsorption or poor response. [1] [9] New hepatitis needs a same-day plan Hold hepatotoxic TB drugs and evaluate when ALT is at least 3 times the upper limit of normal with hepatitis symptoms, or at least 5 times without symptoms. Assess bilirubin, INR and other causes. In severe disease, arrange an active nonhepatotoxic interim combination with a TB expert. Reintroduction is supervised and sequential after recovery; do not leave the patient on an accidentally ineffective partial regimen. [2] With creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min or hemodialysis, pyrazinamide and ethambutol generally require interval adjustment, often three times weekly after dialysis. Isoniazid and rifampin usually retain standard dosing. Confirm the exact weight-based dose and monitoring with pharmacy. [28] [2]

slides.title: Disease site and host factors can override the short-course option
slides.section: Disease site and host factors can override the short-course option
rows: Treat promptly with a CNS-appropriate multidrug regimen, generally a prolonged course such as 9-12 months. Standard pulmonary shortening trials do not apply. Adjunctive corticosteroids are guideline-supported, but HIV-specific evidence and the 2026 genotype trial require careful interpretation.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Disease site and host factors can override the short-course option Situations requiring a different discussion Situation Teaching point TB meningitis Treat promptly with a CNS-appropriate multidrug regimen, generally a prolonged course such as 9-12 months. Standard pulmonary shortening trials do not apply. Adjunctive corticosteroids are guideline-supported, but HIV-specific evidence and the 2026 genotype trial require careful interpretation. Bone, joint or spinal TB Rifamycin-containing therapy is often 6-9 months; many experts favor 9 months, with longer courses in selected circumstances such as extensive hardware. Assess neurologic compromise, instability, large abscesses and need for tissue diagnosis or surgery. Pleural or lymph-node TB Often treatable with a standard six-month course. Enlarging nodes during treatment can be paradoxical, but assess adherence, resistance and other diagnoses before assigning that explanation. TB and HIV Coordinate ART and TB treatment together. Do not remove the rifamycin solely to preserve an incompatible ART regimen without expert review. Low CD4 counts and CNS disease affect eligibility and ART timing. Pregnancy Treat active disease without delay. U.S. guidance individualizes pyrazinamide use; WHO routinely includes it in standard drug-susceptible treatment. Avoid assuming the rifapentine-moxifloxacin or pretomanid regimens are supported in pregnancy. Isoniazid resistance with rifampin susceptibility Do not continue standard HR as if both were active. WHO recommends a six-month rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide and levofloxacin regimen when appropriate susceptibility is established. Check for additional resistance and seek expert input. [2] [22] [23] [8] [21] For patients with HIV who are not receiving ART and do not have TB meningitis, NIH recommends starting ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment if CD4 is below 50 cells/mm³, and within 2-8 weeks if CD4 is at least 50. This is the timing used in the companion HIV module. For TB meningitis, NIH permits ART after at least 2 weeks once meningitis is controlled, while ATS/CDC/IDSA guidance favors waiting 8 weeks. Select and document a CNS-specific plan with the HIV/TB team. [36] [22] Source control in TB is selective Antimicrobial therapy is central. Drainage, decompression or surgery is indicated for specific complications, such as neurologic compromise, mechanical instability, selected abscesses or empyema, rather than for every residual lesion. Obtain tissue for histology, mycobacterial culture and DST when diagnosis remains uncertain. Coordinate specimen handling so the only diagnostic sample is not placed entirely in formalin. [2] [5]

[2] [22] [23] [8] [21] For patients with HIV who are not receiving ART and do not have TB meningitis, NIH recommends starting ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment if CD4 is below 50 cells/mm³, and within 2-8 weeks if CD4 is at least 50. This is the timing used in the companion HIV module. For TB meningitis, NIH permits ART after at least 2 weeks once meningitis is controlled, while ATS/CDC/IDSA guidance favors waiting 8 weeks. Select and document a CNS-specific plan with the HIV/TB team. [36] [22] Source control in TB is selective Antimicrobial therapy is central. Drainage, decompression or surgery is indicated for specific complications, such as neurologic compromise, mechanical instability, selected abscesses or empyema, rather than for every residual lesion. Obtain tissue for histology, mycobacterial culture and DST when diagnosis remains uncertain. Coordinate specimen handling so the only diagnostic sample is not placed entirely in formalin. [2] [5]

slides.section: Read the endpoint before accepting a shorter treatment claim
paragraphs: Noninferiority means that the confidence interval stayed within a prespecified margin for a specified endpoint in a specified population. It does not establish identical efficacy, prove superiority or show that the regimen works at every disease site. A composite outcome can include loss to follow-up, treatment changes and death as well as microbiologic failure.
Phase 3 RCT
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Read the endpoint before accepting a shorter treatment claim Noninferiority means that the confidence interval stayed within a prespecified margin for a specified endpoint in a specified population. It does not establish identical efficacy, prove superiority or show that the regimen works at every disease site. A composite outcome can include loss to follow-up, treatment changes and death as well as microbiologic failure. Phase 3 RCT Study 31/A5349 established an eligible four-month option Among 2,516 randomized participants, the four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen had unfavorable outcomes in 15.5% versus 14.6% with standard therapy in the microbiologically eligible population. The reported difference was 1.0 percentage point, 95% CI -2.6 to 4.5, within a 6-percentage-point noninferiority margin. The rifapentine regimen without moxifloxacin did not establish noninferiority. Practice implication: use the complete studied regimen in eligible pulmonary TB. The result does not support arbitrary four-month courses, and the trial exclusions remain clinically important. [10] [4] Randomized trial TB-PRACTECAL changed the burden of resistant-TB treatment The 2022 report evaluated 24-week BPaLM against 9-20 months of standard care. Of 301 stage-2 participants, 128 were included in the modified intention-to-treat efficacy population. Unfavorable outcomes at 72 weeks occurred in 11% versus 48%; the risk difference was -37 percentage points, 96.6% CI -53 to -22. Grade 3 or higher or serious adverse events occurred in 19% versus 59%. The comparator, open-label design, early stopping and composite endpoint matter. This was a major efficacy/tolerability advance over the comparator regimens, but the 37-point difference should not be described as a mortality benefit or as a comparison against every modern oral regimen. [11] Dose/duration RCT ZeNix helped reduce linezolid exposure while preserving activity All 181 participants received bedaquiline and pretomanid; linezolid was randomized to 1,200 or 600 mg daily for 26 or 9 weeks. Favorable outcomes were 93%, 89%, 91% and 84%, respectively. In the 600-mg/26-week group, peripheral neuropathy occurred in 24% and myelosuppression in 2%. This supports the current lower-dose approach and intensive toxicity surveillance. It was not a comparison of BPaL with an external standard-care control, and four modest-sized groups cannot exclude important efficacy differences. [12] [1] Phase 3 RCT endTB provided several nine-month alternatives The trial randomized 754 participants with fluoroquinolone-susceptible RR pulmonary TB; 699 entered the modified intention-to-treat analysis. At week 73, the control favorable-outcome rate was 80.7%. Differences versus control were +9.8 points for BCLLfxZ (95% CI 0.9 to 18.7), +8.3 for BLMZ (-0.8 to 17.4), and +4.6 for BDLLfxZ (-4.9 to 14.1). These three regimens had consistent noninferiority support across analyses, using a 12-point margin. DCMZ met the modified intention-to-treat criterion but was not supported by the per-protocol analysis. Grade 3 or higher adverse events were common across arms. This trial expands options; it does not establish that nine-month therapy is preferable to BPaLM. [13] Phase 3 RCT · 2026 BEAT-TB supports a pretomanid-free six-month strategy This pragmatic South African trial randomized 403 participants to six-month bedaquiline, delamanid and linezolid with levofloxacin and/or clofazimine, adjusted to susceptibility, or the local standard strategy. Treatment success sustained through week 76 occurred in 174/202 (86.1%) versus 172/200 (86.0%). The adjusted difference was -0.2 points, 95% CI -6.9 to 6.5, meeting the trial noninferiority criterion. The study included groups often excluded elsewhere, including pregnancy and people with HIV. Inclusion does not make every subgroup estimate precise. Its comparator was not BPaLM. WHO incorporated the underlying BEAT evidence into 2025 recommendations before this 2026 journal publication. [14] [9]
