slides.title: The next advances must demonstrate durable cure and acceptable toxicity
slides.section: The next advances must demonstrate durable cure and acceptable toxicity
paragraphs: Investigational strategy
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
The next advances must demonstrate durable cure and acceptable toxicity Investigational strategy TRUNCATE-TB is not routine two-month treatment The strategy trial included 674 participants in its intention-to-treat population. Initial eight-week bedaquiline-linezolid, with isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, was followed by extension for persistent disease, surveillance and retreatment for relapse. At week 96, death, ongoing treatment or active TB occurred in 5.8% versus 3.9% with standard treatment. The adjusted difference was 0.8 points, 97.5% CI -3.4 to 5.1. Mean total treatment time was 85 versus 180 days. [15] The 2025 regimen analysis used a different question. Unfavorable outcomes, mainly relapse, occurred in 26/189 (14%) on the bedaquiline-linezolid regimen versus 7/181 (4%) with standard therapy; adjusted difference 9.3 points, 95% Bayesian credible interval 4.3 to 14.9. Successful retreatment could rescue the strategy outcome while the initial regimen still had more relapses. Do not present these results as equivalent durable cure after eight weeks. [16] Phase 2b/c · 2026 Quabodepistat offers a new target and a rifamycin-free combination Quabodepistat inhibits DprE1, a cell-wall synthesis target. A proof-of-concept trial randomized 122 participants with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB to four months of delamanid-bedaquiline-quabodepistat at three dose levels or six months of standard treatment. In the modified intention-to-treat population, end-of-treatment sputum culture conversion was 96/100 (96%) across pooled experimental groups and 21/21 (100%) in control. The difference was -4.0 points, with an 80% CI of -7.4 to 3.4, meeting its 12-point margin. This is encouraging regimen-development evidence, not proof of equal relapse-free cure. The small control arm, pooled doses, surrogate primary endpoint and 80% rather than 95% interval limit certainty. It does not establish effectiveness in drug-resistant or extrapulmonary TB, and it is not a routine prescribing option. [17] Phase 2b dose finding Sutezolid aims to improve on linezolid's therapeutic window PanACEA-SUDOCU-01 randomized 75 participants to different sutezolid doses or no sutezolid on a bedaquiline-delamanid-moxifloxacin background. The pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model estimated a 16.7% increase in time-to-positivity slope steepness at exposure typical of 1,200 mg, 95% CI 0.7 to 35.0, relative to no exposure. No neuropathy was reported. This is a model-based bacteriologic effect, not a 16.7% improvement in cure. The study did not establish a final dose, durable-cure advantage or comparative long-course safety against linezolid. Sutezolid remains a research option. [18] Phase 2 early activity Telacebec demonstrates activity without establishing a treatment regimen In a 64-patient randomized trial, telacebec 100, 200 or 300 mg daily was compared with standard four-drug treatment for 14 days. At 300 mg, the mean daily decline in sputum bacterial load was 0.097 log CFU versus 0.200 with the four-drug control. Phase 2b dose finding

Complete source section:
The next advances must demonstrate durable cure and acceptable toxicity Investigational strategy TRUNCATE-TB is not routine two-month treatment The strategy trial included 674 participants in its intention-to-treat population. Initial eight-week bedaquiline-linezolid, with isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, was followed by extension for persistent disease, surveillance and retreatment for relapse. At week 96, death, ongoing treatment or active TB occurred in 5.8% versus 3.9% with standard treatment. The adjusted difference was 0.8 points, 97.5% CI -3.4 to 5.1. Mean total treatment time was 85 versus 180 days. [15] The 2025 regimen analysis used a different question. Unfavorable outcomes, mainly relapse, occurred in 26/189 (14%) on the bedaquiline-linezolid regimen versus 7/181 (4%) with standard therapy; adjusted difference 9.3 points, 95% Bayesian credible interval 4.3 to 14.9. Successful retreatment could rescue the strategy outcome while the initial regimen still had more relapses. Do not present these results as equivalent durable cure after eight weeks. [16] Phase 2b/c · 2026 Quabodepistat offers a new target and a rifamycin-free combination Quabodepistat inhibits DprE1, a cell-wall synthesis target. A proof-of-concept trial randomized 122 participants with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB to four months of delamanid-bedaquiline-quabodepistat at three dose levels or six months of standard treatment. In the modified intention-to-treat population, end-of-treatment sputum culture conversion was 96/100 (96%) across pooled experimental groups and 21/21 (100%) in control. The difference was -4.0 points, with an 80% CI of -7.4 to 3.4, meeting its 12-point margin. This is encouraging regimen-development evidence, not proof of equal relapse-free cure. The pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model estimated a 16.7% increase in time-to-positivity slope steepness at exposure typical of 1,200 mg, 95% CI 0.7 to 35.0, relative to no exposure. No neuropathy was reported. This is a model-based bacteriologic effect, not a 16.7% improvement in cure. The study did not establish a final dose, durable-cure advantage or comparative long-course safety against linezolid. Sutezolid remains a research option. [18] Phase 2 early activity Telacebec demonstrates activity without establishing a treatment regimen In a 64-patient randomized trial, telacebec 100, 200 or 300 mg daily was compared with standard four-drug treatment for 14 days. At 300 mg, the mean daily decline in sputum bacterial load was 0.097 log CFU versus 0.200 with the four-drug control. Activity was dose-dependent and tolerability was favorable during this short observation period. The study confirms human antimycobacterial activity of an energy-production target. It does not establish monotherapy as treatment, a cure rate, resistance protection or safety over months. Combination studies with relapse follow-up are needed. slides.title: Telacebec demonstrates activity without establishing a treatment regimen
slides.section: The next advances must demonstrate durable cure and acceptable toxicity
paragraphs: Negative phase 3 result
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
The next advances must demonstrate durable cure and acceptable toxicity Investigational strategy TRUNCATE-TB is not routine two-month treatment The strategy trial included 674 participants in its intention-to-treat population. Initial eight-week bedaquiline-linezolid, with isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, was followed by extension for persistent disease, surveillance and retreatment for relapse. At week 96, death, ongoing treatment or active TB occurred in 5.8% versus 3.9% with standard treatment. The adjusted difference was 0.8 points, 97.5% CI -3.4 to 5.1. Mean total treatment time was 85 versus 180 days. [15] The 2025 regimen analysis used a different question. Unfavorable outcomes, mainly relapse, occurred in 26/189 (14%) on the bedaquiline-linezolid regimen versus 7/181 (4%) with standard therapy; adjusted difference 9.3 points, 95% Bayesian credible interval 4.3 to 14.9. Successful retreatment could rescue the strategy outcome while the initial regimen still had more relapses. Do not present these results as equivalent durable cure after eight weeks. [16] Phase 2b/c · 2026 Quabodepistat offers a new target and a rifamycin-free combination Quabodepistat inhibits DprE1, a cell-wall synthesis target. A proof-of-concept trial randomized 122 participants with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB to four months of delamanid-bedaquiline-quabodepistat at three dose levels or six months of standard treatment. In the modified intention-to-treat population, end-of-treatment sputum culture conversion was 96/100 (96%) across pooled experimental groups and 21/21 (100%) in control. The difference was -4.0 points, with an 80% CI of -7.4 to 3.4, meeting its 12-point margin. This is encouraging regimen-development evidence, not proof of equal relapse-free cure. The small control arm, pooled doses, surrogate primary endpoint and 80% rather than 95% interval limit certainty. It does not establish effectiveness in drug-resistant or extrapulmonary TB, and it is not a routine prescribing option. [17] Phase 2b dose finding Sutezolid aims to improve on linezolid's therapeutic window PanACEA-SUDOCU-01 randomized 75 participants to different sutezolid doses or no sutezolid on a bedaquiline-delamanid-moxifloxacin background. The pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model estimated a 16.7% increase in time-to-positivity slope steepness at exposure typical of 1,200 mg, 95% CI 0.7 to 35.0, relative to no exposure. No neuropathy was reported. This is a model-based bacteriologic effect, not a 16.7% improvement in cure. The study did not establish a final dose, durable-cure advantage or comparative long-course safety against linezolid. Sutezolid remains a research option. [18] Phase 2 early activity Telacebec demonstrates activity without establishing a treatment regimen In a 64-patient randomized trial, telacebec 100, 200 or 300 mg daily was compared with standard four-drug treatment for 14 days. At 300 mg, the mean daily decline in sputum bacterial load was 0.097 log CFU versus 0.200 with the four-drug control. Activity was dose-dependent and tolerability was favorable during this short observation period. The study confirms human antimycobacterial activity of an energy-production target. It does not establish monotherapy as treatment, a cure rate, resistance protection or safety over months. Combination studies with relapse follow-up are needed. [19] Negative phase 3 result HARVEST did not show a survival benefit from high-dose rifampin in TB meningitis In 499 adults, adding rifampin to reach 35 mg/kg daily for 8 weeks was compared with 10 mg/kg daily, both within multidrug treatment. Six-month mortality estimates were 44.6% versus 40.7%; hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.54, P=0.25. Improved drug exposure is not itself clinical benefit. This trial does not support routine high-dose oral rifampin to improve adult TB-meningitis survival. The interval also does not prove the two strategies equally safe. [20] Host-directed therapy needs the same evidentiary discipline In the 2026 genotype-stratified dexamethasone trial in HIV-negative TB meningitis, neither noninferiority nor superiority of placebo was established in the LTA4H CC/CT groups. This does not justify routine genotype-guided steroid omission. Serious adverse events were similar, 52.8% with dexamethasone versus 51.9% with placebo. [21] For other host-directed agents or long-acting formulations, distinguish preclinical activity, exposure studies and registered trials from demonstrated patient benefit. A proposed anti-inflammatory mechanism or convenient dosing interval is not a reason to add a drug to a standard regimen. For every new avenue, ask whether it reduces relapse, death, toxicity or treatment burden, and whether resistance was measured. This is a selected evidence review, not an exhaustive inventory of every compound in development. No unpublished cure rates are assumed.

In the modified intention-to-treat population, end-of-treatment sputum culture conversion was 96/100 (96%) across pooled experimental groups and 21/21 (100%) in control. The difference was -4.0 points, with an 80% CI of -7.4 to 3.4, meeting its 12-point margin. This is encouraging regimen-development evidence, not proof of equal relapse-free cure. The small control arm, pooled doses, surrogate primary endpoint and 80% rather than 95% interval limit certainty. It does not establish effectiveness in drug-resistant or extrapulmonary TB, and it is not a routine prescribing option. [17] Phase 2b dose finding Sutezolid aims to improve on linezolid's therapeutic window PanACEA-SUDOCU-01 randomized 75 participants to different sutezolid doses or no sutezolid on a bedaquiline-delamanid-moxifloxacin background. The pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model estimated a 16.7% increase in time-to-positivity slope steepness at exposure typical of 1,200 mg, 95% CI 0.7 to 35.0, relative to no exposure. No neuropathy was reported. This is a model-based bacteriologic effect, not a 16.7% improvement in cure. The study did not establish a final dose, durable-cure advantage or comparative long-course safety against linezolid. Sutezolid remains a research option. [18] Phase 2 early activity Telacebec demonstrates activity without establishing a treatment regimen In a 64-patient randomized trial, telacebec 100, 200 or 300 mg daily was compared with standard four-drug treatment for 14 days. At 300 mg, the mean daily decline in sputum bacterial load was 0.097 log CFU versus 0.200 with the four-drug control. Activity was dose-dependent and tolerability was favorable during this short observation period. The study confirms human antimycobacterial activity of an energy-production target. It does not establish monotherapy as treatment, a cure rate, resistance protection or safety over months. Combination studies with relapse follow-up are needed. [19] Negative phase 3 result HARVEST did not show a survival benefit from high-dose rifampin in TB meningitis In 499 adults, adding rifampin to reach 35 mg/kg daily for 8 weeks was compared with 10 mg/kg daily, both within multidrug treatment. Six-month mortality estimates were 44.6% versus 40.7%; hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.54, P=0.25. Improved drug exposure is not itself clinical benefit. This trial does not support routine high-dose oral rifampin to improve adult TB-meningitis survival. The interval also does not prove the two strategies equally safe. [20] Host-directed therapy needs the same evidentiary discipline In the 2026 genotype-stratified dexamethasone trial in HIV-negative TB meningitis, neither noninferiority nor superiority of placebo was established in the LTA4H CC/CT groups. This does not justify routine genotype-guided steroid omission. Serious adverse events were similar, 52.8% with dexamethasone versus 51.9% with placebo. [21] For other host-directed agents or long-acting formulations, distinguish preclinical activity, exposure studies and registered trials from demonstrated patient benefit. A proposed anti-inflammatory mechanism or convenient dosing interval is not a reason to add a drug to a standard regimen. For every new avenue, ask whether it reduces relapse, death, toxicity or treatment burden, and whether resistance was measured. This is a selected evidence review, not an exhaustive inventory of every compound in development. No unpublished cure rates are assumed.

slides.title: Preventive treatment is a different treatment problem
slides.section: Preventive treatment is a different treatment problem
paragraphs: Exclude active TB before prescribing preventive monotherapy or dual therapy. Symptoms, radiographic abnormalities or significant immunosuppression may require sputum testing even when the referral says “latent TB.” [24]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Preventive treatment is a different treatment problem Exclude active TB before prescribing preventive monotherapy or dual therapy. Symptoms, radiographic abnormalities or significant immunosuppression may require sputum testing even when the referral says “latent TB.” [24] Common preventive regimens Regimen Course Selection issue 3HP Isoniazid + rifapentine weekly for 3 months, 12 doses CDC option from age 2 years. Check ART interactions. Not recommended during pregnancy or when pregnancy is expected during treatment. 4R Rifampin daily for 4 months Often useful in HIV-negative adults and children. Check all interacting medications and source-case resistance. 3HR Isoniazid + rifampin daily for 3 months Option for adults and children, including selected people with HIV when interactions permit. 6H / 9H Isoniazid daily for 6 or 9 months Alternatives when rifamycin interactions or other constraints preclude short-course therapy; generally less favorable completion and toxicity profiles. 1HP Isoniazid + rifapentine daily for 1 month WHO option, with evidence and age/ART restrictions. It is not the same as 3HP and is not listed as a standard regimen on the CDC general LTBI page. 6Lfx after MDR/RR-TB exposure Levofloxacin daily for 6 months WHO-recommended prevention after appropriate exposure evaluation. Exclude disease and review source-case susceptibility, particularly FQ resistance, with the TB program. [24] [26] [25] The VQUIN and TB-CHAMP pooled analysis combined trials enrolling 2,041 and 922 contacts, respectively. By 54 weeks, TB developed in 8 levofloxacin recipients versus 21 placebo recipients. Low event counts limit precision, and tolerability and adherence remain relevant. This supports a prevention pathway after resistant-TB exposure, not levofloxacin monotherapy for active disease. [27] Turn a positive test into a complete preventive-care plan First exclude disease. Then establish exposure timing, source-case susceptibility, prior treatment, pregnancy status, liver risk and all medications. Recent contacts and people facing substantial immunosuppression deserve prompt coordination. Prefer a short rifamycin regimen when feasible; interactions may favor isoniazid instead. Rifampin plus pyrazinamide is not an LTBI regimen because of hepatotoxicity. [35] Common adult preventive doses; verify weight and interactions Course Adult dose Scheduled doses 3HP Isoniazid 15 mg/kg, rounded up to nearest 50 or 100 mg, maximum 900 mg; rifapentine 900 mg when weight ≥50 kg. Lower weights need the CDC weight-band table. Both once weekly ×12. This is not daily active-TB rifapentine dosing. 4R Rifampin 10 mg/kg, maximum 600 mg daily. 120 daily doses. 3HR Isoniazid 5 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg, plus rifampin 10 mg/kg, maximum 600 mg daily. 90 daily doses. 6H / 9H Isoniazid 5 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg daily. 180 / 270 daily doses. These are adult schedules; children need pediatric dosing. Add pyridoxine with isoniazid for neuropathy risk, including pregnancy, HIV, diabetes, malnutrition and renal disease, commonly 25–50 mg/day. [24] [2] Review adherence, new TB symptoms and toxicity monthly. Obtain baseline AST/ALT and bilirubin for hepatic risk, HIV, pregnancy or the first three postpartum months; repeat for abnormal baseline values, ongoing risk or symptoms. Give explicit stop-and-call instructions for hepatitis symptoms, rash, or persistent neuropathy. [24] Discuss rifamycin interactions with ART, anticoagulants, transplant drugs and contraception before prescribing. Document the infection test, disease-exclusion assessment, regimen, doses completed and completion date. Do not use a repeat IGRA/TST as a cure test. Many pregnant patients can defer prevention until 2–3 months postpartum, but recent exposure or high progression risk can favor treatment during pregnancy. Avoid 3HP during pregnancy; coordinate high-risk decisions with the TB program. [35] [30] [23]

slides.title: Turn a positive test into a complete preventive-care plan
slides.section: Preventive treatment is a different treatment problem
paragraphs: First exclude disease. Then establish exposure timing, source-case susceptibility, prior treatment, pregnancy status, liver risk and all medications. Recent contacts and people facing substantial immunosuppression deserve prompt coordination. Prefer a short rifamycin regimen when feasible; interactions may favor isoniazid instead. Rifampin plus pyrazinamide is not an LTBI regimen because of hepatotoxicity. [35]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Preventive treatment is a different treatment problem Exclude active TB before prescribing preventive monotherapy or dual therapy. Symptoms, radiographic abnormalities or significant immunosuppression may require sputum testing even when the referral says “latent TB.” [24] Common preventive regimens Regimen Course Selection issue 3HP Isoniazid + rifapentine weekly for 3 months, 12 doses CDC option from age 2 years. Check ART interactions. Not recommended during pregnancy or when pregnancy is expected during treatment. 4R Rifampin daily for 4 months Often useful in HIV-negative adults and children. Check all interacting medications and source-case resistance. 3HR Isoniazid + rifampin daily for 3 months Option for adults and children, including selected people with HIV when interactions permit. 6H / 9H Isoniazid daily for 6 or 9 months Alternatives when rifamycin interactions or other constraints preclude short-course therapy; generally less favorable completion and toxicity profiles. 1HP Isoniazid + rifapentine daily for 1 month WHO option, with evidence and age/ART restrictions. It is not the same as 3HP and is not listed as a standard regimen on the CDC general LTBI page. 6Lfx after MDR/RR-TB exposure Levofloxacin daily for 6 months WHO-recommended prevention after appropriate exposure evaluation. Exclude disease and review source-case susceptibility, particularly FQ resistance, with the TB program. [24] [26] [25] The VQUIN and TB-CHAMP pooled analysis combined trials enrolling 2,041 and 922 contacts, respectively. By 54 weeks, TB developed in 8 levofloxacin recipients versus 21 placebo recipients. Low event counts limit precision, and tolerability and adherence remain relevant. This supports a prevention pathway after resistant-TB exposure, not levofloxacin monotherapy for active disease. [27] Turn a positive test into a complete preventive-care plan First exclude disease. Then establish exposure timing, source-case susceptibility, prior treatment, pregnancy status, liver risk and all medications. Recent contacts and people facing substantial immunosuppression deserve prompt coordination. Prefer a short rifamycin regimen when feasible; interactions may favor isoniazid instead. Rifampin plus pyrazinamide is not an LTBI regimen because of hepatotoxicity. [35] Common adult preventive doses; verify weight and interactions Course Adult dose Scheduled doses 3HP Isoniazid 15 mg/kg, rounded up to nearest 50 or 100 mg, maximum 900 mg; rifapentine 900 mg when weight ≥50 kg. Lower weights need the CDC weight-band table. Both once weekly ×12. This is not daily active-TB rifapentine dosing. 4R Rifampin 10 mg/kg, maximum 600 mg daily. 120 daily doses. 3HR Isoniazid 5 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg, plus rifampin 10 mg/kg, maximum 600 mg daily. 90 daily doses. 6H / 9H Isoniazid 5 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg daily. 180 / 270 daily doses. These are adult schedules; children need pediatric dosing. Add pyridoxine with isoniazid for neuropathy risk, including pregnancy, HIV, diabetes, malnutrition and renal disease, commonly 25–50 mg/day. [24] [2] Review adherence, new TB symptoms and toxicity monthly. Obtain baseline AST/ALT and bilirubin for hepatic risk, HIV, pregnancy or the first three postpartum months; repeat for abnormal baseline values, ongoing risk or symptoms. Give explicit stop-and-call instructions for hepatitis symptoms, rash, or persistent neuropathy. [24] Discuss rifamycin interactions with ART, anticoagulants, transplant drugs and contraception before prescribing. Document the infection test, disease-exclusion assessment, regimen, doses completed and completion date. Do not use a repeat IGRA/TST as a cure test. Many pregnant patients can defer prevention until 2–3 months postpartum, but recent exposure or high progression risk can favor treatment during pregnancy. Avoid 3HP during pregnancy; coordinate high-risk decisions with the TB program. [35] [30] [23]

slides.title: Turn a positive test into a complete preventive-care plan
slides.section: Preventive treatment is a different treatment problem
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Preventive treatment is a different treatment problem Exclude active TB before prescribing preventive monotherapy or dual therapy. Symptoms, radiographic abnormalities or significant immunosuppression may require sputum testing even when the referral says “latent TB.” [24] Common preventive regimens Regimen Course Selection issue 3HP Isoniazid + rifapentine weekly for 3 months, 12 doses CDC option from age 2 years. Check ART interactions. Not recommended during pregnancy or when pregnancy is expected during treatment. 4R Rifampin daily for 4 months Often useful in HIV-negative adults and children. Check all interacting medications and source-case resistance. 3HR Isoniazid + rifampin daily for 3 months Option for adults and children, including selected people with HIV when interactions permit. 6H / 9H Isoniazid daily for 6 or 9 months Alternatives when rifamycin interactions or other constraints preclude short-course therapy; generally less favorable completion and toxicity profiles. 1HP Isoniazid + rifapentine daily for 1 month WHO option, with evidence and age/ART restrictions. It is not the same as 3HP and is not listed as a standard regimen on the CDC general LTBI page. 6Lfx after MDR/RR-TB exposure Levofloxacin daily for 6 months WHO-recommended prevention after appropriate exposure evaluation. Exclude disease and review source-case susceptibility, particularly FQ resistance, with the TB program. [24] [26] [25] The VQUIN and TB-CHAMP pooled analysis combined trials enrolling 2,041 and 922 contacts, respectively. By 54 weeks, TB developed in 8 levofloxacin recipients versus 21 placebo recipients. Low event counts limit precision, and tolerability and adherence remain relevant. This supports a prevention pathway after resistant-TB exposure, not levofloxacin monotherapy for active disease. [27] Turn a positive test into a complete preventive-care plan First exclude disease. Then establish exposure timing, source-case susceptibility, prior treatment, pregnancy status, liver risk and all medications. Recent contacts and people facing substantial immunosuppression deserve prompt coordination. Prefer a short rifamycin regimen when feasible; interactions may favor isoniazid instead. Rifampin plus pyrazinamide is not an LTBI regimen because of hepatotoxicity. [35] Common adult preventive doses; verify weight and interactions Course Adult dose Scheduled doses 3HP Isoniazid 15 mg/kg, rounded up to nearest 50 or 100 mg, maximum 900 mg; rifapentine 900 mg when weight ≥50 kg. Lower weights need the CDC weight-band table. Both once weekly ×12. This is not daily active-TB rifapentine dosing. 4R Rifampin 10 mg/kg, maximum 600 mg daily. 120 daily doses. 3HR Isoniazid 5 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg, plus rifampin 10 mg/kg, maximum 600 mg daily. 90 daily doses. 6H / 9H Isoniazid 5 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg daily. 180 / 270 daily doses. These are adult schedules; children need pediatric dosing. Add pyridoxine with isoniazid for neuropathy risk, including pregnancy, HIV, diabetes, malnutrition and renal disease, commonly 25–50 mg/day. [24] [2] Review adherence, new TB symptoms and toxicity monthly. Obtain baseline AST/ALT and bilirubin for hepatic risk, HIV, pregnancy or the first three postpartum months; repeat for abnormal baseline values, ongoing risk or symptoms. Give explicit stop-and-call instructions for hepatitis symptoms, rash, or persistent neuropathy. [24] Discuss rifamycin interactions with ART, anticoagulants, transplant drugs and contraception before prescribing. Document the infection test, disease-exclusion assessment, regimen, doses completed and completion date. Do not use a repeat IGRA/TST as a cure test. Many pregnant patients can defer prevention until 2–3 months postpartum, but recent exposure or high progression risk can favor treatment during pregnancy. Avoid 3HP during pregnancy; coordinate high-risk decisions with the TB program. [35] [30] [23]

slides.title: Case 1. A negative IGRA is not an exit from the workup
slides.section: Apply the regimen and evidence to the bedside
paragraphs: A 47-year-old receiving anti-TNF therapy has 6 weeks of cough, weight loss and an upper-lobe cavity. The IGRA is negative.
Can airborne precautions and the TB evaluation be stopped?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Apply the regimen and evidence to the bedside Case 1. A negative IGRA is not an exit from the workup A 47-year-old receiving anti-TNF therapy has 6 weeks of cough, weight loss and an upper-lobe cavity. The IGRA is negative. Can airborne precautions and the TB evaluation be stopped? Reason through the decision No. Continue the disease evaluation and airborne precautions. Collect appropriate respiratory specimens, NAAT and cultures. Immunosuppression can blunt immune-based tests. Decide on empiric multidrug treatment from the full clinical picture, not the IGRA alone. [5] [6] Case 2. A genuine four-month candidate A 28-year-old, 65-kg patient has pulmonary TB with susceptible testing, no extrapulmonary disease, no pregnancy, no relevant interactions and acceptable QT risk. What is the shorter option, and what is not interchangeable? Reason through the decision Discuss 8 weeks of HPZM followed by 9 weeks of HPM with the TB program. Confirm the full daily 119-dose course and follow-up. Four months of standard RIPE-based therapy or rifapentine without moxifloxacin does not reproduce the evidence. [4] [10] Case 3. Cavitation and a positive two-month culture A patient on standard HRZE had cavitary disease at baseline. The culture obtained at completion of 2 months remains positive and is still drug susceptible. Is this automatically treatment failure? Reason through the decision It is a relapse-risk signal, not automatic failure at two months. Review observed doses, interactions, absorption and DST. With cavitation plus the positive two-month culture, plan a 7-month continuation phase, usually 9 months total, under TB-program direction. [3] [2] Case 4. Rifampin resistance is not solved by adding moxifloxacin A respiratory NAAT detects rifampin resistance. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is pending. What information must guide the next regimen? Reason through the decision Arrange urgent TB-expert consultation, expanded molecular and phenotypic DST, prior-drug history and an active resistant-TB combination. FQ susceptibility distinguishes BPaLM from BPaL eligibility. Pregnancy, disease site and component resistance can rule out both. Do not simply add one drug to HRZE. [7] [1] Case 5. Linezolid toxicity threatens the combination During BPaLM therapy, a patient develops falling hemoglobin and new distal tingling. Cultures have converted. Can linezolid simply be stopped for the remainder? Reason through the decision Assess severity and hold or modify the offending drug when clinically necessary, but make the revised regimen with a TB expert. Culture conversion does not eliminate the need for active companion drugs. Check CBC, neurologic findings, visual symptoms, drug exposure and other causes. The duration of prior linezolid and activity of remaining drugs determine the options. [1] [9] Case 6. An eight-week headline does not establish an eight-week cure A patient asks for the “two-month TB treatment” after reading about TRUNCATE-TB. How would you explain the actual evidence? Reason through the decision The trial shortened initial treatment and then closely monitored patients, extending or restarting therapy when needed. The later analysis found more unfavorable outcomes with the initial short regimen. It is not a routine alternative to the recommended four- or six-month course. [15] [16] Case 7. An AFB-positive result without a TB NAAT signal A 70-year-old with bronchiectasis has chronic cough. The sputum is smear positive but the TB NAAT is negative. Is this confirmed TB? Reason through the decision No. Consider NTM, specimen or assay issues, and the remaining probability of TB. Ask the laboratory about the discordance, collect additional specimens and await identification/culture. Make the isolation decision with IP; one result does not replace the institutional pathway. If NTM is isolated, assess full disease criteria before treating. [29] [32] Case 8. A positive IGRA and a growing lung mass A patient with remote TB exposure has a positive IGRA and an enlarging cavitary lung lesion. Initial sputum studies are unrevealing. Does the IGRA justify closing the differential? Reason through the decision No. Infection testing does not identify the cause of the lesion. Continue a directed TB evaluation and consider tissue for malignancy, fungal infection and other mimics. Coordinate fresh tissue for cultures alongside pathology. [5] [34] Case 9. Prevention before anti-TNF therapy An asymptomatic adult has a positive IGRA before anti-TNF treatment, a normal chest radiograph and no evidence of active disease. What makes a useful LTBI plan? Reason through the decision Choose a compatible short-course regimen when possible after medication and exposure review. Specify doses, monitoring, adherence support and documentation. Coordinate timing of immunosuppression with the treating team; do not apply one universal interval to every biologic and clinical urgency. [35] [24]

slides.title: Reason through the decision
slides.section: Apply the regimen and evidence to the bedside
paragraphs: No. Continue the disease evaluation and airborne precautions. Collect appropriate respiratory specimens, NAAT and cultures. Immunosuppression can blunt immune-based tests. Decide on empiric multidrug treatment from the full clinical picture, not the IGRA alone. [5] [6]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Apply the regimen and evidence to the bedside Case 1. A negative IGRA is not an exit from the workup A 47-year-old receiving anti-TNF therapy has 6 weeks of cough, weight loss and an upper-lobe cavity. The IGRA is negative. Can airborne precautions and the TB evaluation be stopped? Reason through the decision No. Continue the disease evaluation and airborne precautions. Collect appropriate respiratory specimens, NAAT and cultures. Immunosuppression can blunt immune-based tests. Decide on empiric multidrug treatment from the full clinical picture, not the IGRA alone. [5] [6] Case 2. A genuine four-month candidate A 28-year-old, 65-kg patient has pulmonary TB with susceptible testing, no extrapulmonary disease, no pregnancy, no relevant interactions and acceptable QT risk. What is the shorter option, and what is not interchangeable? Reason through the decision Discuss 8 weeks of HPZM followed by 9 weeks of HPM with the TB program. Confirm the full daily 119-dose course and follow-up. Four months of standard RIPE-based therapy or rifapentine without moxifloxacin does not reproduce the evidence. [4] [10] Case 3. Cavitation and a positive two-month culture A patient on standard HRZE had cavitary disease at baseline. The culture obtained at completion of 2 months remains positive and is still drug susceptible. Is this automatically treatment failure? Reason through the decision It is a relapse-risk signal, not automatic failure at two months. Review observed doses, interactions, absorption and DST. With cavitation plus the positive two-month culture, plan a 7-month continuation phase, usually 9 months total, under TB-program direction. [3] [2] Case 4. Rifampin resistance is not solved by adding moxifloxacin A respiratory NAAT detects rifampin resistance. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is pending. What information must guide the next regimen? Reason through the decision Arrange urgent TB-expert consultation, expanded molecular and phenotypic DST, prior-drug history and an active resistant-TB combination. FQ susceptibility distinguishes BPaLM from BPaL eligibility. Pregnancy, disease site and component resistance can rule out both. Do not simply add one drug to HRZE. [7] [1] Case 5. Linezolid toxicity threatens the combination During BPaLM therapy, a patient develops falling hemoglobin and new distal tingling. Cultures have converted. Can linezolid simply be stopped for the remainder? Reason through the decision Assess severity and hold or modify the offending drug when clinically necessary, but make the revised regimen with a TB expert. Culture conversion does not eliminate the need for active companion drugs. Check CBC, neurologic findings, visual symptoms, drug exposure and other causes. The duration of prior linezolid and activity of remaining drugs determine the options. [1] [9] Case 6. An eight-week headline does not establish an eight-week cure A patient asks for the “two-month TB treatment” after reading about TRUNCATE-TB. How would you explain the actual evidence? Reason through the decision The trial shortened initial treatment and then closely monitored patients, extending or restarting therapy when needed. The later analysis found more unfavorable outcomes with the initial short regimen. It is not a routine alternative to the recommended four- or six-month course. [15] [16] Case 7. An AFB-positive result without a TB NAAT signal A 70-year-old with bronchiectasis has chronic cough. The sputum is smear positive but the TB NAAT is negative. Is this confirmed TB? Reason through the decision No. Consider NTM, specimen or assay issues, and the remaining probability of TB. Ask the laboratory about the discordance, collect additional specimens and await identification/culture. Make the isolation decision with IP; one result does not replace the institutional pathway. If NTM is isolated, assess full disease criteria before treating. [29] [32] Case 8. A positive IGRA and a growing lung mass A patient with remote TB exposure has a positive IGRA and an enlarging cavitary lung lesion. Initial sputum studies are unrevealing. Continue a directed TB evaluation and consider tissue for malignancy, fungal infection and other mimics. Coordinate fresh tissue for cultures alongside pathology. [5] [34] Case 9. Reason through the decision Choose a compatible short-course regimen when possible after medication and exposure review. Specify doses, monitoring, adherence support and documentation. Coordinate timing of immunosuppression with the treating team; do not apply one universal interval to every biologic and clinical urgency. [35] [24]

slides.title: Reason through the decision
slides.section: Apply the regimen and evidence to the bedside
paragraphs: It is a relapse-risk signal, not automatic failure at two months. Review observed doses, interactions, absorption and DST. With cavitation plus the positive two-month culture, plan a 7-month continuation phase, usually 9 months total, under TB-program direction. [3] [2]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Apply the regimen and evidence to the bedside Case 1. A negative IGRA is not an exit from the workup A 47-year-old receiving anti-TNF therapy has 6 weeks of cough, weight loss and an upper-lobe cavity. The IGRA is negative. Can airborne precautions and the TB evaluation be stopped? Reason through the decision No. Continue the disease evaluation and airborne precautions. Collect appropriate respiratory specimens, NAAT and cultures. Immunosuppression can blunt immune-based tests. Decide on empiric multidrug treatment from the full clinical picture, not the IGRA alone. [5] [6] Case 2. A genuine four-month candidate A 28-year-old, 65-kg patient has pulmonary TB with susceptible testing, no extrapulmonary disease, no pregnancy, no relevant interactions and acceptable QT risk. What is the shorter option, and what is not interchangeable? Reason through the decision Discuss 8 weeks of HPZM followed by 9 weeks of HPM with the TB program. Confirm the full daily 119-dose course and follow-up. Four months of standard RIPE-based therapy or rifapentine without moxifloxacin does not reproduce the evidence. [4] [10] Case 3. Cavitation and a positive two-month culture A patient on standard HRZE had cavitary disease at baseline. The culture obtained at completion of 2 months remains positive and is still drug susceptible. Is this automatically treatment failure? Reason through the decision It is a relapse-risk signal, not automatic failure at two months. Review observed doses, interactions, absorption and DST. With cavitation plus the positive two-month culture, plan a 7-month continuation phase, usually 9 months total, under TB-program direction. [3] [2] Case 4. Rifampin resistance is not solved by adding moxifloxacin A respiratory NAAT detects rifampin resistance. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is pending. What information must guide the next regimen? Reason through the decision Arrange urgent TB-expert consultation, expanded molecular and phenotypic DST, prior-drug history and an active resistant-TB combination. FQ susceptibility distinguishes BPaLM from BPaL eligibility. Pregnancy, disease site and component resistance can rule out both. Do not simply add one drug to HRZE. [7] [1] Case 5. Linezolid toxicity threatens the combination During BPaLM therapy, a patient develops falling hemoglobin and new distal tingling. Cultures have converted. Can linezolid simply be stopped for the remainder? Reason through the decision Assess severity and hold or modify the offending drug when clinically necessary, but make the revised regimen with a TB expert. Culture conversion does not eliminate the need for active companion drugs. Check CBC, neurologic findings, visual symptoms, drug exposure and other causes. The duration of prior linezolid and activity of remaining drugs determine the options. [1] [9] Case 6. An eight-week headline does not establish an eight-week cure A patient asks for the “two-month TB treatment” after reading about TRUNCATE-TB. How would you explain the actual evidence? Reason through the decision The trial shortened initial treatment and then closely monitored patients, extending or restarting therapy when needed. The later analysis found more unfavorable outcomes with the initial short regimen. It is not a routine alternative to the recommended four- or six-month course. [15] [16] Case 7. An AFB-positive result without a TB NAAT signal A 70-year-old with bronchiectasis has chronic cough. The sputum is smear positive but the TB NAAT is negative. Is this confirmed TB? Reason through the decision No. Consider NTM, specimen or assay issues, and the remaining probability of TB. Ask the laboratory about the discordance, collect additional specimens and await identification/culture. Make the isolation decision with IP; one result does not replace the institutional pathway. If NTM is isolated, assess full disease criteria before treating. [29] [32] Case 8. A positive IGRA and a growing lung mass A patient with remote TB exposure has a positive IGRA and an enlarging cavitary lung lesion. Initial sputum studies are unrevealing. Does the IGRA justify closing the differential? Reason through the decision No. Infection testing does not identify the cause of the lesion. Continue a directed TB evaluation and consider tissue for malignancy, fungal infection and other mimics. Coordinate fresh tissue for cultures alongside pathology. [5] [34] Case 9. Prevention before anti-TNF therapy An asymptomatic adult has a positive IGRA before anti-TNF treatment, a normal chest radiograph and no evidence of active disease. What makes a useful LTBI plan? Reason through the decision Choose a compatible short-course regimen when possible after medication and exposure review. Specify doses, monitoring, adherence support and documentation. Coordinate timing of immunosuppression with the treating team; do not apply one universal interval to every biologic and clinical urgency. [35] [24]

slides.title: Reason through the decision
slides.section: Apply the regimen and evidence to the bedside
paragraphs: Assess severity and hold or modify the offending drug when clinically necessary, but make the revised regimen with a TB expert. Culture conversion does not eliminate the need for active companion drugs. Check CBC, neurologic findings, visual symptoms, drug exposure and other causes. The duration of prior linezolid and activity of remaining drugs determine the options. [1] [9]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Apply the regimen and evidence to the bedside Case 1. A negative IGRA is not an exit from the workup A 47-year-old receiving anti-TNF therapy has 6 weeks of cough, weight loss and an upper-lobe cavity. The IGRA is negative. Can airborne precautions and the TB evaluation be stopped? Reason through the decision No. Continue the disease evaluation and airborne precautions. Collect appropriate respiratory specimens, NAAT and cultures. Immunosuppression can blunt immune-based tests. Decide on empiric multidrug treatment from the full clinical picture, not the IGRA alone. [5] [6] Case 2. A genuine four-month candidate A 28-year-old, 65-kg patient has pulmonary TB with susceptible testing, no extrapulmonary disease, no pregnancy, no relevant interactions and acceptable QT risk. What is the shorter option, and what is not interchangeable? Reason through the decision Discuss 8 weeks of HPZM followed by 9 weeks of HPM with the TB program. Confirm the full daily 119-dose course and follow-up. Four months of standard RIPE-based therapy or rifapentine without moxifloxacin does not reproduce the evidence. [4] [10] Case 3. Cavitation and a positive two-month culture A patient on standard HRZE had cavitary disease at baseline. The culture obtained at completion of 2 months remains positive and is still drug susceptible. Is this automatically treatment failure? Reason through the decision It is a relapse-risk signal, not automatic failure at two months. Review observed doses, interactions, absorption and DST. With cavitation plus the positive two-month culture, plan a 7-month continuation phase, usually 9 months total, under TB-program direction. [3] [2] Case 4. Rifampin resistance is not solved by adding moxifloxacin A respiratory NAAT detects rifampin resistance. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is pending. What information must guide the next regimen? Reason through the decision Arrange urgent TB-expert consultation, expanded molecular and phenotypic DST, prior-drug history and an active resistant-TB combination. FQ susceptibility distinguishes BPaLM from BPaL eligibility. Pregnancy, disease site and component resistance can rule out both. Do not simply add one drug to HRZE. [7] [1] Case 5. Linezolid toxicity threatens the combination During BPaLM therapy, a patient develops falling hemoglobin and new distal tingling. Cultures have converted. Can linezolid simply be stopped for the remainder? Reason through the decision Assess severity and hold or modify the offending drug when clinically necessary, but make the revised regimen with a TB expert. Culture conversion does not eliminate the need for active companion drugs. Check CBC, neurologic findings, visual symptoms, drug exposure and other causes. The duration of prior linezolid and activity of remaining drugs determine the options. [1] [9] Case 6. An eight-week headline does not establish an eight-week cure A patient asks for the “two-month TB treatment” after reading about TRUNCATE-TB. How would you explain the actual evidence? Confirm the full daily 119-dose course and follow-up. Four months of standard RIPE-based therapy or rifapentine without moxifloxacin does not reproduce the evidence. [4] [10] Case 3. Cavitation and a positive two-month culture A patient on standard HRZE had cavitary disease at baseline. The culture obtained at completion of 2 months remains positive and is still drug susceptible. Is this automatically treatment failure? Reason through the decision It is a relapse-risk signal, not automatic failure at two months. Review observed doses, interactions, absorption and DST. With cavitation plus the positive two-month culture, plan a 7-month continuation phase, usually 9 months total, under TB-program direction. [3] [2] Case 4. Rifampin resistance is not solved by adding moxifloxacin A respiratory NAAT detects rifampin resistance. Fluoroquinolone susceptibility is pending. What information must guide the next regimen? Reason through the decision Arrange urgent TB-expert consultation, expanded molecular and phenotypic DST, prior-drug history and an active resistant-TB combination. FQ susceptibility distinguishes BPaLM from BPaL eligibility. Pregnancy, disease site and component resistance can rule out both. Do not simply add one drug to HRZE. [7] [1] Case 5. Linezolid toxicity threatens the combination During BPaLM therapy, a patient develops falling hemoglobin and new distal tingling. Cultures have converted. Can linezolid simply be stopped for the remainder? Reason through the decision Assess severity and hold or modify the offending drug when clinically necessary, but make the revised regimen with a TB expert. Culture conversion does not eliminate the need for active companion drugs. Check CBC, neurologic findings, visual symptoms, drug exposure and other causes. The duration of prior linezolid and activity of remaining drugs determine the options. [1] [9] Case 6. An eight-week headline does not establish an eight-week cure A patient asks for the “two-month TB treatment” after reading about TRUNCATE-TB. How would you explain the actual evidence? Reason through the decision The trial shortened initial treatment and then closely monitored patients, extending or restarting therapy when needed. The later analysis found more unfavorable outcomes with the initial short regimen. It is not a routine alternative to the recommended four- or six-month course. [15] [16] Case 7. An AFB-positive result without a TB NAAT signal A 70-year-old with bronchiectasis has chronic cough. The sputum is smear positive but the TB NAAT is negative. Is this confirmed TB? Reason through the decision No. Consider NTM, specimen or assay issues, and the remaining probability of TB. Ask the laboratory about the discordance, collect additional specimens and await identification/culture. Make the isolation decision with IP; one result does not replace the institutional pathway. If NTM is isolated, assess full disease criteria before treating. [29] [32] Case 8. A positive IGRA and a growing lung mass A patient with remote TB exposure has a positive IGRA and an enlarging cavitary lung lesion. Initial sputum studies are unrevealing. Does the IGRA justify closing the differential? Reason through the decision No. Infection testing does not identify the cause of the lesion. Continue a directed TB evaluation and consider tissue for malignancy, fungal infection and other mimics. Coordinate fresh tissue for cultures alongside pathology. [5] [34] Case 9. Prevention before anti-TNF therapy An asymptomatic adult has a positive IGRA before anti-TNF treatment, a normal chest radiograph and no evidence of active disease. What makes a useful LTBI plan? Reason through the decision Choose a compatible short-course regimen when possible after medication and exposure review. Specify doses, monitoring, adherence support and documentation. Coordinate timing of immunosuppression with the treating team; do not apply one universal interval to every biologic and clinical urgency. [35] [24]

paragraphs: Communicate the disease classification, infectiousness assessment, regimen and its rationale, completed doses, pending resistance results, toxicity plan and person responsible for follow-up. A prescription without an access and follow-up plan is incomplete.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
A useful consult note specifies what happens next Communicate the disease classification, infectiousness assessment, regimen and its rationale, completed doses, pending resistance results, toxicity plan and person responsible for follow-up. A prescription without an access and follow-up plan is incomplete. Suspected/confirmed TB at [site], with [microbiology and resistance results]. Airborne precautions [status and criteria to reassess with infection prevention]. Regimen [full drug names, doses, start date and rationale]. Pending tests [culture, molecular and phenotypic DST, other sites]. Monitoring [specific tests, next date and clinician/program reviewing them]. Duration [provisional course and findings that would change it]. Public-health coordination [program, contact and plan for DOT/vDOT]. Discharge [medication supply, follow-up, household risk assessment and transport plan]. Clinical implementation Confirm current isolation rules, laboratory testing, reporting, TB-program consultation, and drug access with the treating institution. A lecture summary does not establish an isolation decision.

slides.title: Check that you can explain the decisions
slides.section: Check that you can explain the decisions
paragraphs: Pause before reading each answer. These are discussion questions for individual study or facilitated teaching.
1. Why should a positive NAAT still be followed by culture?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Check that you can explain the decisions Pause before reading each answer. These are discussion questions for individual study or facilitated teaching. 1. Why should a positive NAAT still be followed by culture? Answer and rationale Culture supports organism recovery, susceptibility testing and response assessment. A molecular result does not replace those functions. [5] 2. Which two findings commonly extend the standard pulmonary course to nine months? Answer and rationale Baseline cavitation plus a positive sputum culture at completion of two months. Investigate adherence, susceptibility and exposure as part of the same decision. [3] 3. How does daily rifapentine for active TB differ from 3HP? Answer and rationale The active-TB regimen uses daily rifapentine within HPZM/HPM for 17 weeks. 3HP uses weekly isoniazid-rifapentine for prevention. Neither the schedules nor the treatment purposes are interchangeable. [4] 4. When does BPaL replace BPaLM in the U.S. guideline? Answer and rationale In otherwise eligible rifampin-resistant pulmonary disease with fluoroquinolone resistance or intolerance. Component activity and other eligibility restrictions still apply. slides.section: TB on rounds: diagnose, distinguish, treat
paragraphs: Adult-oriented memory aid • September 21, 2026 • Use with the eligibility and dosing details in the full module.
Consider NTM, endemic fungi, bacterial abscess/emboli, Nocardia, cancer and inflammatory disease. IGRA positivity does not explain a lesion; target culture and tissue.
Exclude active disease first. Prefer eligible 3HP, 4R or 3HR; use 6H/9H when appropriate. Check interactions, source resistance and pregnancy; arrange monthly review.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
TB on rounds: diagnose, distinguish, treat Adult-oriented memory aid • September 21, 2026 • Use with the eligibility and dosing details in the full module. Do not anchor on TB Consider NTM, endemic fungi, bacterial abscess/emboli, Nocardia, cancer and inflammatory disease. IGRA positivity does not explain a lesion; target culture and tissue. Treat latent infection Exclude active disease first. Prefer eligible 3HP, 4R or 3HR; use 6H/9H when appropriate. Check interactions, source resistance and pregnancy; arrange monthly review. Recognize and isolate Suspected pulmonary/laryngeal TB: airborne precautions, appropriate respirator and prompt IP/TB-program contact. IGRA/TST cannot rule out disease. Get the right samples Sputum AFB smear/culture, typically three specimens 8-24 h apart with one early morning; respiratory NAAT and rapid resistance testing. Preserve culture for DST. Drug-susceptible pulmonary TB Standard 2HRZE/4HR. Eligible age ≥12, weight ≥40 kg: 8 weeks HPZM then 9 weeks HPM. Pregnancy, most extrapulmonary disease, interactions or resistance may preclude shortening. Reassess duration For the standard regimen, cavitation plus positive culture at 2 months usually means 9 months total. Review doses, DST and exposure. CNS and bone/joint disease need site-specific plans. Rifampin-resistant disease Urgent expert input. FQ susceptible: consider BPaLM; FQ resistant/intolerant: consider BPaL if otherwise eligible. U.S. guidance uses 26 weeks. Never add one drug to failure. Monitor the combination Monthly response/adherence review and sputum cultures until conversion. Liver tests; CBC/neuropathy/vision for linezolid; vision for ethambutol; ECG and K+/Mg2+/Ca2+ for QT-active regimens. Sources and evidence boundaries Reviewed September 15, 2026. Guidelines and primary studies are linked below. Numerical trial summaries use the populations and endpoints named in the text. Some newer reports were available as abstracts; detailed eligibility and prescribing decisions should use the complete trial protocol and current guidance. No faculty approval or local-policy verification is implied. ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA treatment update . 2025. Guideline. Four-month drug-susceptible treatment, pediatric shortening, BPaL/BPaLM and monitoring. ATS/CDC/IDSA drug-susceptible TB guideline . 2016. Guideline. Standard treatment, dose adjustment, toxicity, extrapulmonary disease and response assessment. CDC treatment of drug-susceptible TB . April 17, 2025. U.S. implementation guidance. CDC rifapentine-moxifloxacin implementation guidance . February 25, 2022. Eligibility, exclusions, doses and 119-dose schedule. CDC clinical and laboratory diagnosis . Current online guidance. Specimen collection, NAAT, culture and resistance testing. CDC prevention of TB transmission in health-care settings . 2005. Hospital airborne precautions. Apply the current institutional implementation policy. CDC drug-resistant TB treatment . Current online guidance. U.S. approach to resistant disease and expert consultation. WHO consolidated guidelines, module 4, treatment and care . 2025. WHO recommendations; these do not establish U.S. regulatory approval or local availability. WHO operational handbook, six-month resistant-TB regimens . 2025. BDLLfxC selection, fluoroquinolone-based adjustment, subgroups and duration. Dorman et al. Study 31/A5349 . 2021. Randomized phase 3 noninferiority trial. Four-month rifapentine regimens with or without moxifloxacin. Nyang’wa et al. TB-PRACTECAL . 2022. Randomized trial. A 24-week all-oral regimen for rifampin-resistant TB. Numerical results here refer to the 2022 report. Conradie et al. ZeNix . 2022. Randomized linezolid dose/duration trial within BPaL. Guglielmetti et al. endTB . January 30, 2025. Randomized phase 3 trial of nine-month oral regimens for fluoroquinolone-susceptible RR-TB. Conradie et al. BEAT Tuberculosis . June 25, 2026. Pragmatic randomized phase 3 trial of a six-month strategy for RR-TB. Published abstract and WHO implementation materials reviewed. Paton et al. TRUNCATE-TB strategy trial . 2023. Randomized strategy trial with extension, monitoring and retreatment. Paton et al. TRUNCATE-TB regimen analysis . 2025. Prespecified exploratory analysis of initial eight-week regimens, distinct from the strategy outcome. Dawson et al. Quabodepistat-delamanid-bedaquiline . May 29, 2026. Randomized phase 2b/c proof-of-concept study. Published abstract reviewed; no claim of full-text/supplement review. Heinrich et al. PanACEA-SUDOCU-01 . Online July 8, 2025. Randomized phase 2b dose-finding study. Published abstract reviewed. Janssen et al. Telacebec phase 2 trial . 2025. Randomized 14-day early bactericidal activity study. Published abstract reviewed. Meya et al. HARVEST . December 18, 2025. Randomized trial of high-dose oral rifampin in adult TB meningitis. Published abstract reviewed. Donovan et al. Genotype-stratified adjunctive dexamethasone . Online January 15, 2026. Randomized phase 3 trial in HIV-negative adults with TB meningitis. Published abstract reviewed. CDC care for people with TB and HIV . April 17, 2025. HIV-specific treatment considerations and links to NIH guidance. CDC TB treatment during pregnancy . Current online guidance. U.S. approach, including individualized pyrazinamide use. CDC treatment for latent TB infection . Current online guidance. Preferred short rifamycin-based regimens, exclusions and monitoring. WHO preventive treatment options . 2024 update. Recommendation for six months of levofloxacin after MDR/RR-TB exposure. WHO recommended preventive regimens . 2024 update. Includes 1HP and comparison of preventive regimens. Duong et al. VQUIN and TB-CHAMP individual-participant meta-analysis . Online December 18, 2024. Randomized preventive-treatment evidence in household contacts, distinct from active-TB treatment. WHO drug-susceptible TB in special situations . 2025. Renal and hepatic considerations; used here for renal dosing and monitoring. ATS/CDC/IDSA diagnosis of TB in adults and children . 2017. Diagnostic guideline: discordant results, specimen selection and interpretation. CDC IGRA clinical testing guidance . Current online guidance. Immune-test interpretation, limitations and repeat testing. CDC tuberculin skin testing guidance . Current online guidance. Reading and risk-based thresholds. ATS/ERS/ESCMID/IDSA NTM pulmonary disease guideline . 2020. Distinguishing NTM isolation from pulmonary disease. CDC histoplasmosis testing algorithm . May 13, 2024. Endemic fungal testing and antigen/antibody limitations. Gadkowski and Stout. Cavitary pulmonary disease . 2008. Background differential diagnosis; not used for current treatment recommendations. NTCA/CDC latent TB treatment recommendations . 2020. Regimen selection, benefits, interactions and toxicity. NIH adult and adolescent OI guidance, Mycobacterium tuberculosis . Updated May 2, 2024; reviewed by NIH March 16, 2026. ART timing and TB/HIV interactions; checked September 15, 2026.
